lessons.name: What is a database and why not just use files?
lessons.desc: A database is an organized collection of structured data managed by a DBMS. Files work for tiny projects but break down fast — no fast search, no concurrent access, no integrity rules.
lessons.q: What is a database? Why do we need one instead of just using files?
lessons.qsub: What happens when two users try to write to the same CSV file at the same time?
terms: Structured data ka organized collection — DBMS se manage.
Software jo data store/query/update karta hai — PostgreSQL, MySQL.
Data maangne ka sawal — SQL mein likha jo hai.
Kai users ek saath data par kaam karein, bin hahi lade.
lessons.what:
Database = structured data ka collection, jo ek DBMS (jaise PostgreSQL) manage karta hai. Files (CSV/JSON) chhote kaam ke liye theek hain, par asli app mein turant faile hain.

Files ki 4 beemariyan: search slow (puri file padhni padegi), concurrency unsafe (do log ek saath write karein to data gattha), no integrity (koi rule nahi — duplicate ya broken data aasani se aa jata), aur no scale. Database in sab ka ilaaj: index (fast search), locking (safe concurrency), constraints (integrity), transactions (ACID).
lessons.analogy: Zip folder vs coded almirah: zip mein bas files padi hain — dhundhne ke liye sab kholna padega, do log ek saath hi ghus jayenge. Database = almirah jisme index cards hain (turant dhundh), talla (ek time par ek banda), aur register (jo bhi likha, rule se likha).
lessons.why: Sabse pehla "why database?" — interview ka answer 4 shortcomings: search, concurrency, integrity, scale. Baaki sab topics (index, ACID, replication) isi ke answers hain. Root samjho, tree apne aap banta.

lessons.name: Tables, rows, and columns
lessons.desc: A table is the fundamental storage unit — like a spreadsheet with a fixed structure. Columns define the structure with names and data types. Rows hold the actual data.
lessons.q: What is a table? What are columns and rows? How do data types matter?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between schema and data? Why does one table model one entity?
terms: Storage ka fundamental unit — jaise spreadsheet, fixed structure.
Table ka structure — name + data type (INT, TEXT, DATE).
Ek record — columnon ki values ek line mein.
Table ka layout — kaunse columns, kaunse types.
Column ka contract — INTEGER, VARCHAR, BOOLEAN...
lessons.what:
Table spreadsheet jaise hai: columns define karte hain structure (kaunse fields, kaunse types), rows mein data hota hai (har row = ek record). Schema = layout; data = content. In dono ka antar clear rakhna zaroori hai.

Ek table ek entity model karta hai — users table, orders table, products table. Data types column ko contract dete hain: VARCHAR(50) matlab wahi max 50 chars, DECIMAL(10,2) matlab paise. Type galat = data galat.
lessons.analogy: Khali register vs bhara register: schema = khali register ke columns (date, naam, paisa), data = bhare hue rows. Register ka format pehle fix karo, phir likho — yahi table hai.
lessons.why: Har SQL query table ke upar chalti hai. Schema vs data, entity-modeling, data types — interview ke basics hain. "Explain a table like I am 5" ka yahi jaadu: columns = structure, rows = values.

lessons.name: Primary Key — uniquely identifies every row
lessons.desc: A Primary Key uniquely identifies each row. It cannot be NULL, no duplicates allowed. Database auto-creates an index on it for fast O(log n) lookups.
lessons.q: What is a primary key? What properties must it satisfy?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between a natural key and a surrogate key? When would you use UUID vs auto-increment?
terms: Har row ki unique pehchaan — duplicate nahi, NULL nahi.
Constraint — koi value ek baar se zyada na aaye.
Banaayi hui key (auto-increment id, UUID) — koi asli matlab nahi.
Data se aayi key — jaise Aadhaar number, email.
PK par DB khud index banata hai — fast lookup.
lessons.what:
Primary Key (PK) har row ko uniquely pehchanta. Rules: NULL nahi ho sakti, duplicate nahi hoti. DB us par auto index bana deta hai isliye WHERE id = 5 instant hai (O(log n)).

Surrogate (auto-increment, UUID) vs natural (email, Aadhaar): surrogate control mein rehta hai, kabhi change nahi hota. Natural change ho sakti hai (email badlti hai) — isliye production mein surrogate prefer karo.
lessons.analogy: Roll number: school mein har bachche ka roll number alag — yahi PK. Naam same ho sakta hai (2 Rahuls), roll number nahi. Naam = natural key (badal sakta), roll no = surrogate (pakka).
lessons.why: PK ke bina targeting impossible — same rows update/delete ho jayengi. Har relationship (FK) PK ko refer karta hai. Interview ka classic: "UUID vs auto-increment?" — data jo kabhi change nahi hota, wahan natural bhi theek.

lessons.name: Foreign Key — links rows across tables
lessons.desc: A Foreign Key references the Primary Key of another table, creating relationships. Database enforces referential integrity — you cannot create an order for a non-existent user.
lessons.q: What is a foreign key? How does it enforce referential integrity?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE SET NULL? When would you use each?
terms: Column jo doosri table ki PK refer karta — link banata.
Rule: FK value us parent table mein honi hi chahiye.
Parent delete to child bhi delete.
Parent delete to child ka ref NULL ho jaye.
M:N relation ko 2 tables + link table se model karta.
lessons.what:
Foreign Key (FK) ek column hai jo doosri table ki PK ko point karta. Ye relationships banata hai: order tumhara hai, uske user_id se user mil jayega. DB referential integrity enforce karta hai — aisa order create nahi ho sakta jiska user hi na ho.

ON DELETE ka policy set karni padti: CASCADE (user gayab to orders bhi gayab) ya SET NULL (order bachega, user_id NULL ho jayega). Ye chunav business logic par depend karta hai.
lessons.analogy: Pan card + jobs list: adhaar/pancard = PK (unique pehchaan). Jobs list mein "adhaar no" = FK — jo number likha hai wo sach mein aadhaar hai. Agar kabhi galti se galat number daala, to register check karke mana kar dega — yahi referential integrity.
lessons.why: Relationship/join ka adhar FK hai. Merge karte waqt (interview: inner join) DB FK se batata hai kaise jodo. Integrity = data kabhi "air-hostess with no flight" nahi ban sakta.

lessons.name: Your first query — SELECT
lessons.desc: SELECT is how you read data. SELECT * returns all columns. SELECT name, email returns specific columns. SQL execution order: FROM → WHERE → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
lessons.q: How does SELECT work? What is the order of SQL clause execution?
lessons.qsub: Why can you not use a column alias defined in SELECT inside a WHERE clause?
terms: Data padhne ka command — * matlab saare columns.
Kaunse columns dikhane — SELECT name, email.
FROM → WHERE → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT (logical).
lessons.what:
SELECT data padhne ka mantar. SELECT * FROM users = saare columns, SELECT name, email = sirf ye columns (projection). AS se alias de sakte ho — output ka naam badal jaata.

Supreme rule: SQL upar-se-neeche nahi chalta. Logical order: FROM (kis table se) → WHERE (filter) → SELECT (project) → ORDER BY (sort) → LIMIT. Isi liye SELECT mein define alias WHERE mein use nahi ho sakta — alias abhi bana hi nahi.
lessons.analogy: Mandi jaana: pehle decide dalal (shop/FROM), phir chhaan (filter/WHERE), phir uthao jitna chahiye (SELECT), phir line se lao (ORDER), phir sirf 10 le aao (LIMIT). Order hi sab kuch hai.
lessons.why: Har interview SQL question ki base — execution order. "Alias WHERE mein kyu nahi?" ka jawab yahi. SELECT sirf dikhane ke liye galat matlab nahi — ye g** real hai: projection + calculation output filter ke baad hoti.

FROM users
WHERE age > 18
ORDER BY age DESC

lessons.name: Filtering rows — WHERE, AND, OR, NOT
lessons.desc: WHERE filters which rows are returned. Supports comparisons (=, !=, <, >), logical operators (AND, OR, NOT), pattern matching (LIKE), set membership (IN), range (BETWEEN), and null checks.
lessons.q: How does WHERE filter rows? What operators does it support?
lessons.qsub: Why does WHERE email = NULL not work? What should you use instead?
terms: Row filter — only jo condition match, wahi aage jaaye.
Logical combine: sab / koi ek / ulta.
lessons.what:
WHERE rows ko chhaanta hai. Operators: =, !=, <, >, LIKE (pattern), IN (membership), BETWEEN (range), IS NULL (null check), aur AND/OR/NOT se combine.

Classic trap: WHERE email = NULL kabhi nahi chalegi — NULL ek value nahi, "pata nahi" hai. IS NULL use karo. AND ka matlab dono, OR ka matlab koi ek — parentheses se precedence clear rakho.
lessons.analogy: Screening machine (security) aa gaya: jis par jaanch fail → side. AND = "ID check AND bag check" (dono zaroori), OR = "manager se baat OR authorised card" (koi ek kaafi). NULL = jaanch ka exam hi clear nahi hua (IS NULL check).
lessons.why: Jitna kam data WHERE tak pahunchata, utna query fast. Filtering hi on-return. Interview ka favourite edge: NULL comparison, LIKE wildcards, aur predicate push.

SELECT name, age, city
FROM users
WHERE age > 18
  AND (city = 'Delhi' OR city = 'Mumbai')
  AND email IS NOT NULL;

-- pattern + membership
WHERE name LIKE 'A%';        -- 'A' se shuru
WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3);       -- set membership
WHERE age BETWEEN 18 AND 30; -- inclusive range

-- GLTI: WHERE email = NULL;  -- kabhi fail nahi hoga
-- SAHI: WHERE email IS NULL;

LIKE 'A%' index use kar sakta; LIKE '%A' nahi (leading wildcard).
Interview: NOT IN (NULL) hamesha empty — NULL ka 3-value logic.

lessons.name: Basic CRUD — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
lessons.desc: CRUD = Create, Read, Update, Delete. INSERT INTO creates rows, SELECT reads, UPDATE modifies, DELETE removes. Always use WHERE with UPDATE/DELETE or you affect every row.
lessons.q: What are the four CRUD operations? Why must you always use WHERE with UPDATE and DELETE?
lessons.qsub: What is a soft delete pattern? Why is it preferred over hard deletes in production?
terms: DELETE ki jagah flag — deleted_at timestamp; data bacha rehta.
lessons.what:
CRUD = dataset ki char operations: INSERT (create), SELECT (read), UPDATE (update), DELETE (delete). In ke bina koi bhi app nahi chalta.

Golden rule: UPDATE / DELETE mein hamesha WHERE — varna poori table ki values badal/delete ho jayengi. Production mein soft delete prefer: deleted_at column set karo, data history + restore ki suvidha. Hard delete bas wahan jahan privacy/karor (jaise KYC) ke liye zaroori.
lessons.analogy: Register mein entry: INSERT = naya naam likho; SELECT = padho kaun hai; UPDATE = naam ke aage "married" likho; DELETE = page hi faad do (hard!) vs soft = page bacha, naam ke saath ✗ mark. Koi bhi ladai audit ke liye mark wala option behtar.
lessons.why: Interview "write CRUD for a user" — basic competency. Par asli trick: WHERE ke bina UPDATE/DELETE (banana bug) aur soft-delete pattern. Ye production experience dikhata hai, saath mein follow-up "why soft delete?".

lessons.name: DDL — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
lessons.desc: DDL defines database schema. CREATE TABLE with column types and constraints (PK, FK, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT). ALTER TABLE for modifications. DROP removes objects entirely.
lessons.q: What are the DDL commands? How do constraints like CHECK and UNIQUE work?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between TRUNCATE and DELETE? Why can TRUNCATE not be rolled back in some databases?
terms: Data Definition Language — schema banata/badalta: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE.
Object ko poora hata dena — table jaata bhi hai.
Table ka poora DATA hatao, structure bachao.
lessons.what:
DDL = schema bowl ke commands. CREATE TABLE naaya table banata hai with column types + constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT, NOT NULL). ALTER TABLE se column add/remove/drop aur constraints badalte hain. DROP puri table (data + structure) utha leta hai.

TRUNCATE vs DELETE — samajhna zaroori: DELETE rows conditional (WHERE), transaction ke saath, slow (row-by-row), triggers fire. TRUNCATE instant, table ka data sab hatata, kai DB mein transaction-rollback nahi hota, FK par fail. Production DEMO queries ke liye TRUNCATE behtar.
lessons.analogy: Building contractors: CREATE = naya cowna bpaste (foundation + floors). ALTER = ek floor rename/remove karo, window nai lagao. DROP = poora building utha lo (plot khali). TRUNCATE = building hai par andar ka ferrier sab nikal do — sifren door.
lessons.why: Schema design interview ka jul#1 topic: "constraints kya hain?" aur "TRUNCATE vs DELETE?" — precise answers yahan se. Migrations (ALTER) ka sahi tarika production career ki zaroorat.

lessons.name: DML — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE patterns
lessons.desc: DML operates on row data. SELECT retrieves, INSERT adds, UPDATE modifies, DELETE removes. UPSERT patterns handle duplicate keys. RETURNING clause returns affected rows.
lessons.q: What are the DML commands? How does UPSERT work in PostgreSQL vs MySQL?
lessons.qsub: When would you use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE vs a separate UPDATE query?
terms: Data Manipulation Language — rows par kaam: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
Insert karo, duplicate ho to update — ON CONFLICT (PG), ON DUPLICATE KEY (MySQL).
Multi-row INSERT ya many rows one go.
lessons.what:
DML rows ke saath khelta hai — SELECT (padho), INSERT (jodo), UPDATE (badlo), DELETE (hatao). DDL schema bowl par kaam karta, DML data par.

Interview aur production ke patterns: UPSERT — pehli baar insert, duplicate par update. PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET .... MySQL: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE. Aur RETURNING clause affected rows deta hai (bina extra SELECT ke). Bulk inserts (200 rows ek INSERT mein) row-by-row se kaafi fast.
lessons.analogy: Diary mein note: SELECT = padho, INSERT = naya page, UPDATE = galti sudhaaro (eraser se), DELETE = page faado. UPSERT = "pehle check karo kya naam hai? agar hai to details update karo varana girjao". RETURNING = change ke baad "ab kitna hua?" turant bolna.
lessons.why: Interview warm-up questions yahan se — insert/update/delete with correct syntax, upsert pattern. Ye skill har day-to-day backend kaam hai. "How do you handle duplicate inserts?" — upsert ka jawab high signal.

lessons.name: SELECT execution order
lessons.desc: SQL does not run top-to-bottom. Fixed logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Aliases defined in SELECT are not available in WHERE.
lessons.q: What is the logical execution order of a SQL SELECT query?
lessons.qsub: Why can you not use a column alias from SELECT in a WHERE clause? In which clauses can you use aliases?
terms: SQL ka asli execution sequence — FROM se shuru, LIMIT par khatam.
Table/s source — pehle banata hai working set.
Grouping ke baad HAVING filter karta hai groups ko.
Duplicates hatao — SELECT ke bad, ORDER se pehle.
SELECT ke alias = sirf SELECT/ORDER BY mein; WHERE/GROUP BY mein nahi.
lessons.what:
SQL visually upar-se-neeche dikhta hai par logically alag order chalta hai: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.

Isko samajhna isliye critical: aliases SELECT mein bante hain — isliye WHERE unhe use nahi kar sakta (WHERE pehle gaya), ORDER BY use kar sakta (bad mein). Filters (WHERE) rows ko pehle kam karte hain, phir grouping, phir HAVING groups ko chhaanta.
lessons.analogy: Khana banane ki line: pehle purse se saamaan nikalo (FROM) → Khaara saamaan hatao (WHERE) → dhabba banao (GROUP BY) → dhabbe saaf karo (HAVING) → parosi kya dikhana (SELECT) → lines mein sajao (ORDER BY) → sirf 5 log dikhao (LIMIT). Sale justify meine protocol: agli dahi idhar.
lessons.why: "Why can't I use alias in WHERE?" — sabse asked SQL question. Execution order ka frame hone se set-ology aur query rewriting dono clear. Explain to interviewer in order, ek-ek karke.

lessons.name: JOINs — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS, SELF
lessons.desc: JOINs combine rows from multiple tables based on related columns. INNER JOIN returns only matching rows. LEFT JOIN returns all left rows with NULLs for missing matches. Self-join joins a table with itself.
lessons.q: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN? When would you use each?
lessons.qsub: What is a self-join? How do you find employees and their managers from the same table?
terms: Sirf matching pairs — jinke dono tables mein hai.
Left table ke saare + right ke matching (nahi to NULL).
Right table ke saare + left ke matching.
Dono ke saare row, missing side NULL (combine).
Har left row × har right row — cartesian.
Table ko khud se jodna — jaise manager-employee.
lessons.what:
JOIN alag tables ke rows ko related column par jodta hai. INNER = sirf dono mein matching. LEFT = left sab + right matching, missing ko NULL. RIGHT ulta. FULL = sab quirks dono side. CROSS = har combinations (bina condition). SELF = same table do baar alias karke.

Classic example: employees table mein manager sama column hamesha employee id hota hai — JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id. Interview ka favourite.
lessons.analogy: Dosti list fusion: INNER = woh dono lists mein hain; LEFT = tumhari list thodi khao, agar uski list mein na ho to box empty (NULL); FULL = dono lists ke total unique log, jahan dusra na ho wahan blinda. SELF = ek hi list ko "bos" aur "junior" bana ke compare.
lessons.why: JOIN relational DB ki superpower hai. Interview query questions 80% joins ke around. INNER vs LEFT ka antar = NULL handling — jahan bhi "sab left-side chahiye" (yeh bhi jinke match na ho), wahan LEFT JOIN.

lessons.name: Aggregation — COUNT, SUM, AVG, GROUP BY, HAVING
lessons.desc: GROUP BY collapses many rows into one per unique value. Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) calculate per group. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, unlike WHERE which filters before.
lessons.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING? When do you use each?
lessons.qsub: Why does COUNT(*) count all rows but COUNT(column) exclude NULLs? What is the difference?
terms: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX — many rows → one number.
Rows ko group karna — har group par aggregate.
Groups ka filter — aggregate ke baad.
WHERE = rows (group se pehle), HAVING = groups (baad).
* sab rows count; col NULLs ko skip.
lessons.what:
Aggregates bahut-saari rows -> ek value. COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. GROUP BY rows ko groups mein todta hai aur har group par aggregate chalta hai — GROUP BY dept + COUNT(*) = har department ka count.

HAVING groups ko filter karta hai (aggregate ke baad), WHERE rows ko before group. COUNT(*) sab rows, COUNT(col) NULL ko skip. Yaad rakhna: aggregate ke saath non-grouped column SELECT karna = error.
lessons.analogy: Matia groups mein scoreboard: GROUP BY = teams banaya (par team=login); SUM = har team ka total score; HAVING = sirf teams dikhao jinka total > 100. WHERE pehle un players ko hata deta jo khel nahi paate; HAVING baad mein teams ko.
lessons.why: Analytics queries ki jaan hai aggregation. "dept-wise count", "avg salary per city" — every interview SQL round ka core. WHERE vs HAVING ek-line diff: rows vs groups.

lessons.name: Subqueries & CTEs
lessons.desc: Subqueries are queries inside other queries. CTEs (WITH keyword) give subqueries a name for readability. Correlated subqueries reference outer query columns and execute row-by-row.
lessons.q: What is the difference between a correlated subquery and a regular subquery?
lessons.qsub: Why is EXISTS typically faster than IN for large subquery result sets?
terms: Query ke andar query — parentheses mein.
WITH clause — subquery ko naam + re-use de.
Outer query ke column reference karta; har row par run.
Exist check — subquery row deti hai? turant stop.
IN = list member; EXISTS = exists check, aksar fast.
lessons.what:
Subquery = query ke andar ek aur query. CTE (WITH x AS (...)) subquery ko naam deta hai — readable, reusable. Correlated subquery outer rows ka reference leta hai, isliye har outer row ke liye chal sakta hai.

Inline filter mein EXISTS aksar IN se fast hai — EXISTS "row mila" update karke turant rukta, IN poori list bana ke compare karta. Jaise hi subquery se match mila, ruk jaate ho.
lessons.analogy: Form mein internal exam marks: subquery = "pehle marks nikal lo, phir bara query use kare". CTE = us nikal ke koi na dijiye "MarksReport" naam — baad mein baar-baar use ho. Correlated = har bachche ke liye separately iska marks wala section check karna (ek-ek karke).
lessons.why: Modular query building — complex features (top-per-group, filtering by aggregate) yahan se. CTE readability + performance, interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki complex ko simple components mein todte ho.

lessons.name: Set operations — UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT
lessons.desc: Set operations combine results from multiple SELECTs. UNION merges without duplicates (requires sort). UNION ALL concatenates with duplicates (faster). INTERSECT returns common rows. EXCEPT returns rows in first but not second.
lessons.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL? When would you use each?
lessons.qsub: How would you find customers who bought product A but NOT product B?
terms: Result sets ko vertically jodo — duplicates hatao.
Saare milao — duplicates bhi, fast (no sort).
Pehle set mein hai, dusre mein nahi.
lessons.what:
Set operations do result sets ko milate hain: UNION (common dedup), UNION ALL (sab rakhne), INTERSECT (common), EXCEPT (pehle ke andar, dusre ke bahar). Columns count/types same honi chahiye.

UNION vs UNION ALL: UNION dedup karne ke liye sort/dedup karta hai = slow; UNION ALL sirf concatenate = fast. Jab pata ho duplicates nahi hain, UNION ALL lo. Classic interview: "customers who bought A but not B" → SELECT ... EXCEPT SELECT ....
lessons.analogy: Do class ki student lists: UNION = dono mila ke unique naam (ek hi baar jo dono me hai). UNION ALL = sab naam likhdo, jo dono mein hai wo do baar. INTERSECT = jo dono lists mein same naam hai. EXCEPT = class A ke wo bacche jo class B mein nahi.
lessons.why: Multi-condition queries (yan "ya toh ye ya wo data") set ops se clean sound. UNION for dedup vs UNION ALL performance — interview bit. INTERSECT/EXCEPT simple diff tool queries.

lessons.name: What is an Index? — when to add one, B-tree vs hash (concept)
lessons.desc: An index is a data structure that speeds up row lookups at the cost of slower writes. Without an index, the database scans every row (sequential scan). With an index, it jumps directly to the matching rows. Think of a book index — instead of reading every page, you look up the topic and go straight there.
lessons.q: What is a database index? When should you add one and when should you not?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between a B-tree index and a hash index? When would you use each? What happens to write performance when you add too many indexes?
terms: Data structure jo lookups ko fast karta — book index jaisa.
Bina index — har row padho (slow pada large table).
Har insert/update par index update bhi hota — writes slow.
lessons.what:
Index = book ka index. Bina uske DB har row ko dhundhta hai (sequential scan — madam sab padho). Index ke saath DB seedha matching rows par. Default most databases: B-tree (sorted tree) — equality + range dono ke liye.

Lekin har cheez free nahi: har INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE par index bhi update hota hai — writes slow. Zyada indexes = zyada storage + slow writes. Balance: hot queries ke liye index, write-heavy chhoti tables mein kam.
lessons.analogy: Library bina index: book dhundhne ke liye har shelf ulatna (seq scan). With card catalogue (index): "Sharma, R — shelf 3, row 4" — seedha. Par har nayi book aane par catalogue card update karna padta (write cost).
lessons.why: Timed: index interview ka #1 database topic. "Why index?" → categorize. "When to add?" → read-heavy + WHERE-predicate columns. B-tree vs hash — different access patterns. Performance = index ki madad se query planning.

lessons.name: B-Tree & B+Tree — structure, fanout, range scans
lessons.desc: B+ Trees are the default index in most databases. Self-balancing trees with data only in leaf nodes, which are linked for fast range scans. Height is 3-4 for billions of rows — very few disk seeks.
lessons.q: How does a B+ Tree index work? Why is it efficient for both lookups and range scans?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between B-Tree and B+ Tree? Why do databases prefer B+ Tree?
terms: Default index — sorted tree; data sirf leaves mein, leaves linked.
Har node mein kitne children — bada = tree chhota.
Leaf linked list se aage-piche walk — fast.
Root se leaf tak levels — billions rows par 3-4.
B-tree: data har node mein. B+: sirf leaf mein. B+ range scan behtar.
lessons.what:
B+ Tree relaional DB ka default index hai. Data sirf leaf nodes mein, internal nodes sirf keys (guide). Leaves linked list se jude hote hain isliye range scans ([1,10]) aasani se — ek leaf se agla leaf pe jaakar. Fanout bada hone se tree ki height chhoti — 1 billion rows par bhi 3-4 disk seeks par target paz â.

B-Tree mein data har node mein hota — point lookups theek, par range scan ke liye parent par vaapas jana padta (slow). Isliye B+ Tree databases ka favourite.
lessons.analogy: Railway division maps: hark particular zone mein aana to internal node (route map), asli station (data) leaf par. Zones linked hain isliye "station 5 se 15 tak" bina ghuma seedha leaf-walk se. Do maps: data sab pages par (B-tree) vs sirf station pages par (B+).
lessons.why: Index interview ka core — B+ Tree kyun, fanout kya, range kyun fast. Disk I/O = seeks process; chhoti height = kam seeks. Ye explain karna = senior level signal.

lessons.name: LSM-Tree — memtable, SSTable, compaction
lessons.desc: LSM-Trees make writes super fast by writing to memory first (memtable), then flushing sorted files (SSTables) to disk. Background compaction merges SSTables. Trade-off: reads check multiple files.
lessons.q: How does an LSM-Tree optimize write performance? What is the write path?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between size-tiered and leveled compaction? How do bloom filters help LSM reads?
terms: Write-optimized structure — memory pehle, phir sorted files.
RAM mein sorted collection — writes yahan.
Sorted string table — disk par sorted file.
Jo file mein key ho sakti hai, batata — read ko fast.
lessons.what:
LSM-Tree (Log-Structured Merge) writes ko ultra-fast banata. Write path: pehle memtable (RAM mein sorted) — instant ack. Bharte hi SSTable (sorted file) disk par flush. Background compaction chhoti files ko eco sorted files mein merges karta hai.

Reads ki qeemat: key kaafi si files mein ho sakti hai — isliye Bloom filters batate "is file mein key ho sakti hai ya nahi". Yam si sab files check karo. Tune-offs: size-tiered (sirf same-size merge) vs leveled (level-by-level, cleaner). Ye hi Cassandra/RocksDB/SQLite-WAL ka engine hai.
lessons.analogy: Chhoti tare paapadi stang: khana turant likh do saaf parchment (memtable/RAM) par, kahin jaana nahi (fast ack). Paper bhara to band pate ki files (SSTables) mein. Shaam ko saari files ekatthi kar ke saaf karo (compaction). Dhundhte waqt pehle ram (memtable) dekho, phir files, par bloom filter batata hai kisi file mein jaana hai ya nahi.
lessons.why: Write-heavy systems (Cassandra, RocksDB, DynamoDB) LSM kyun use karte — interview deep-dive. B-tree vs LSM tradeoff: B-tree reads tez writes khatarbaaz; LSM writes chic cheep. "Why Kafka-style appends ultra fast?" — yahi logic.

lessons.name: Buffer pool — LRU, dirty pages, checkpoints
lessons.desc: The buffer pool is the database RAM cache. Reads check memory first (cache hit = instant). On miss, reads from disk, stores in pool. When full, evicts least recently used page. Target: 95%+ hit rate.
lessons.q: What is a buffer pool? How does it improve database performance?
lessons.qsub: What are dirty pages? What is a checkpoint and why does it cause I/O spikes?
terms: DB ka RAM cache — pages yaad rahne.
Page RAM mein mil gaya — no disk read.
RAM mein change hua par disk par likha nahi.
Least Recently Used — kam use wala page nikalo.
Dirty pages ko disk par bolna — jhank jhank ke.
lessons.what:
Buffer pool database ki RAM cache hai. Har read pehle RAM mein dekhta hai (hit = instant, miss = disk). Full hone par allocation kam use (LRU) page ko nikaalta hai.

Dirty pages wo hain jo RAM mein badal gaye par disk par nahi likhe — unhe crash par lena padta. Checkpoint dirty pages ko disk par stabke force karta hai taaki crash-recovery chhoti ho. Target: 95%+ hit rate — iske neeche = kam RAM, zyada I/O cost.
lessons.analogy: Kitchen counter + fridge: daily use saamaan counter (buffer pool) par — turant milta. Rare saamaan fridge (disk) se. Counter bhar jaye to sabse purana use saamaan fridge mein (LRU). "Khaana ghrr but recipe change ho chuki" = dirty page — raat ko saaf karte ho (checkpoint) taaki kal subah entry clean hai.
lessons.why: Disk I/O = slowest. Buffer pool jitna hit, utna tez DB. Interview: cache hit ratio metric, dirty pages/checkpoint aur I/O spike — production operation ka signal. Ye bhi batata hai kyun DB seedha "memory" par chalti hai.

lessons.name: Hash indexes — O(1) point lookups
lessons.desc: Hash indexes map keys to disk locations via hash function — instant O(1) exact-match lookups. Cannot support range queries because hashing scrambles order. Good for WHERE email = x.
lessons.q: When would you use a hash index instead of a B-Tree index?
lessons.qsub: What is extendible hashing? How does it handle bucket overflow gracefully?
terms: Key ka hash -> bucket location — exact match O(1).
Hash collision wale keys saath rehte.
Buckets split jab overflow — directory pointer grow.
Ek hash compute, ek jagah — fast point read.
lessons.what:
Hash index key ko hash function se bucket mein map karta hai — exact match WHERE email = x par O(1). B-tree ki tarah log(n) walk nahi — ek jump. Par range queries (BETWEEN) hash se impossible: hash order tod deta hai.

Extendible hashing bucket overflow handle karta: bucket split hoti, directory (pointer list) grow hota. Practically hash indexes rare (PG hashm access method), par concept se pata chalta hai ki exact-match fast kyun hai.
lessons.analogy: Lockers ka index: naam ka pehla akshar compute karke seedha locker block mein jaao (hash) — ek step, limit. Par "wo sab log jin ka naam R se T ke beech hai" (range) nahi nikal sakte — lockers hash order mein na hone se scattered. Book index (B-tree) uske liye.
lessons.why: Interview: "hash vs B-tree index?" — use cases: equality-heavy (cache, kv lookups) vs range. Ye bhi batata hai ki har data structure ka ek khula maidan hota hai.

lessons.name: Bitmap indexes — low-cardinality columns
lessons.desc: Bitmap indexes store a bit array per distinct value — each bit says if a row has that value. ANDing bitmaps finds intersections instantly. Only useful for columns with few distinct values (status, region).
lessons.q: What is a bitmap index? When is it useful and when is it not?
lessons.qsub: How do you combine multiple bitmap indexes for complex boolean queries?
terms: Har distinct value ke liye bit array — 1 = row par wo value.
Kam distinct values (status, gender) — bitmap gold.
Do bitmaps ka intersect — index par fatafat AND.
lessons.what:
Bitmap index ek value ke liye ek bit array rakhta hai: 1 karta ha array ke ith index par agar row mein wo value hai. WHERE status = 'active' AND tier = 'gold' → dono bitmaps ka AND — CPU par bitwise op, turant result. Isliye low-cardinality columns (status, region, gender) par kamaal.

High-cardinality (email, timestamp) par bitmap khud bhaari ho jaata — har value ke liye apna array. Data warehouses (OLAP) mein popular; OLTP mein rare.
lessons.analogy: 400 baal wej language register: har banda ek bit ked. "Kaun log Delhi se?" = ek column with 1s. "Industry tech AND Delhi" = dono columns ki AND — fast. Par agar har person ki unique city ho to har city ke liye alag column — 1000 columns — waste.
lessons.why: OLAP/columnar conversations mein aata hai — "how does warehouse filter fast on low-cardinality?" Bitmap AND ke saath Jaap is line se patta chalta hai. Ye bhi "when NOT to index" ka example.

lessons.name: Window functions — ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK
lessons.desc: Window functions calculate across related rows without collapsing them like GROUP BY. ROW_NUMBER gives unique numbers. RANK gives ties the same number with gaps. DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps.
lessons.q: What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK?
lessons.qsub: Why can you not use a window function directly in a WHERE clause? How do you filter on window function results?
terms: Har row ke liye, apne "window" (neighbour rows) par calc — rows collapse nahi (GROUP BY ke viprit).
Har row ko unique number — koi bhi 2 same nahi.
Ties ko same rank par gap ke saath: 1,1,3.
Ties ko same rank, koi gap nahi: 1,1,2.
Window define — partition mein divide, order se rank.
lessons.what:
Window functions har row apne window (related rows) ke relative mein calculate karti hain — aur rows collapse nahi hoti (GROUP BY ke viprit). OVER() window define, PARTITION BY group (jaise per-dept), ORDER BY sequence.

ROW_NUMBER = unique numbers (1,2,3). RANK = ties same, gap: 1,1,3. DENSE_RANK = ties same, no gap: 1,1,2. Classic: "har department ka top-3" — window se rank kro phir filter (subquery).
lessons.analogy: Runners ke race mein gota thali: ROW_NUMBER = sab ko ticket do (1,2,3,4). RANK = do bhaag ke same time (tie) to dono ko 2, aur agla 4 (gap). DENSE_RANK = dono 2, agla 3 (no gap, sabko thikane). Podium ke liye — sirf top 3 chahiye to window se nikalo.
lessons.why: GROUP BY rows ko ek line mein khol deta; window har original row ko rakhke per-group rankings de sakta. "Top-N per group", "running totals", "moving average" — window hi solution. Interview is topic par 2-3 level jata hai.

lessons.name: Recursive CTEs — tree/graph traversal
lessons.desc: Recursive CTEs call themselves — perfect for hierarchical data like org charts. Has an anchor member (starting row) and recursive step (joins back to CTE). Runs until no new rows are produced.
lessons.q: How does a recursive CTE work? What are the anchor and recursive members?
lessons.qsub: How would you find all ancestors in a tree? What prevents infinite loops in recursive CTEs?
terms: WITH RECURSIVE — CTE apne aap ko call kare.
CTE se join karke agli layer — tree/chart nikalna.
Jab koi naya row na bane, loop rukta.
lessons.what:
Recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) wahi query hai jo apne aap ko refer karti hai — hierarchical data (org chart, category tree, graph) ke liye perfect. Do members:

1) Anchor — shuru ke rows (jaise top manager). 2) Recursive member — anchor ke results ko CTE se join karke agli level. Itna chalta hai jab tak naya row na bane (termination). Har round par duplicate na ho to loop infinite? Careful: PTs cycle ghisha sakte — visited/level column rakho.
lessons.analogy: Paarivar ki family-tree search: start dada (anchor). "Jis-ka manager ye hai" = recursive step — har person ke manager milte jaate ho. Line khatam (koi manager nahi) to ruk gaye. Cycle (X ka manager Y, Y ka X) — loop hona bad: ek "seen list" rakho.
lessons.why: Interview me tree/graph problem (all manager chain) — recursive CTE hi ek-line SQL solution. Ye ware un-graph anki expected samajh aati hai — "find all ancestors" repeated question.

WITH RECURSIVE org_tree AS (
  -- anchor: top boss
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS level
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  -- recursive: join back to CTE
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, t.level + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN org_tree t ON e.manager_id = t.id

lessons.name: Indexes — B-Tree, Hash, Composite, Covering
lessons.desc: Indexes accelerate data access. B-Tree for range and equality. Composite index on (a,b,c) follows leftmost prefix rule. Covering index includes all columns needed — no table lookup required.
lessons.q: What is the leftmost prefix rule for composite indexes? Give an example.
lessons.qsub: What is a covering index? How does it eliminate key lookups entirely?
terms: Ek index multi-column par — (a, b, c).
Index ke left side se hi start ho sakta — bina a ke b/c nahi.
Saare needed columns index mein — table hit nahi, index-only.
Query ka data index par hi — fastest read.
Kitne distinct values — high = behtar index.
lessons.what:
Composite index = multiple columns par ek index (a,b,c). Query leftmost prefix follow karni padti: a, a,b, a,b,c use hoga, par WHERE b = 1 ya c = 2 akele index miss karta hai.

Covering index us index ko bolte jo query ke saare columns cover karta — DB table ki taraf jaane ki zaroorat nahi (index-only scan), read ultra fast. Tradeoff: jitna bada index, utna storage + writes.
lessons.analogy: Phone book (last_name, first_name) sorted: last se dhundhna tez (prefix). Sirf first name se dhundhna (b,c) = index kaam nahi. Covering = "phone book mein hi number + zip mila", ab aage poora address dhunda. Index hi kaafi tha.
lessons.why: Index interview ka vikas — sirf "add index" nahi, balki kaunsa column order + covering ki soch. Leftmost prefix = classic ask. Jis column par filter/join dono hai usko pehle rakhna.

lessons.name: Query optimization — EXPLAIN ANALYZE
lessons.desc: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows how the database executes your query with actual timing. Seq Scan on large tables = missing index. Index Scan = using an index (fast). Compare estimated vs actual rows for stale statistics.
lessons.q: How do you read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE output? What should you look for?
lessons.qsub: What does a Seq Scan on a million-row table indicate? How do you fix it?
terms: Query plan batata — DB kya strategy choose karega.
Poora table padhna — large table par red flag.
Estimates vs real — stale stats ka (jaadati hai).
lessons.what:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE aksar query ke execution plan ke saath actual timings dikhata hai. Kyun slow — wo jaante ho: Seq Scan (puri million-row table scan) = missing/ineffective index. Index Scan/Index Only Scan = dhundhte hue exception.

Compare karo rows (estimate) vs actual — bade gap par stats stale ya cast galat. Filter reduction%. Memory par sort/hash = memory knol. Seedha: "kahan se sab row aa rahe, kahan karte ho."
lessons.analogy: Google Maps route: EXPLAIN = route ka plan "ye raste se jaaoge" (full scan vs index). ANALYZE = "kiya aur 12ms laga" (real). Pehle route dekho — agar "pura sheher ghumana" phrase dikhe to rasta badlo (index lagao).
lessons.why: Performance jaadu nahi — plan padhna hai. Interview: "query slow, kaise debug?" — EXPLAIN ANALYZE = first tool. Sr. luk nahi "add index", luk ke lights plan. isi skill se index/statistics shabd sahi jagah lagte.

lessons.name: Views & Materialized Views
lessons.desc: Views are saved queries — virtual tables for readability and security. Materialized Views store actual results on disk for fast reads but data goes stale. Must REFRESH to update.
lessons.q: What is the difference between a regular view and a materialized view?
lessons.qsub: When would you use a materialized view instead of a regular view? What are the staleness trade-offs?
terms: Saved query — virtual table; data store nahi hota, har baar run.
Query ka result disk par — fast read, par stale.
Mat view ko update karna (manual ya scheduled).
View columns chhipa sakta — row-level too.
M.V. ka data apni timeline ke peechhe — REFRESH ka intezar.
lessons.what:
View = ek saved query jo table ki tarah dikhta hai. Har SELECT us par query fir chalata — naye data ka live picture. Use: complexity chhipana, consistent interface, security (sirf kuch columns).

Materialized View result ko disk par save karta — reads instant (poora query nahi chalta), par data stale — REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW se update karo. Use: expensive aggregations, reporting jahan slight delay acceptable.
lessons.analogy: Live recording vs photograph: View = live camera feed — jab dekho tab wahi real state. Materialized view = printed photo — bahut jaldi dikhta hai par shaadi ke baad bhi wahi purana shot; nayi photo (REFRESH) khinchwani padegi. Reports = prints, dashboards = live.
lessons.why: Interview: "view vs materialized view" — ek-line diff: live query vs cached snapshot. Ye also example hai read-optimization ka bina kahe. Staleness tradeoff bolna = production awareness.

visual.cap: View = live query. Mat view = stored snapshot + REFRESH.

lessons.name: Stored Procedures, Functions, Triggers
lessons.desc: Stored Procedures are saved SQL code blocks with parameters and logic. Functions return a value and can be used in SELECT. Triggers fire automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE events.
lessons.q: What is the difference between a stored procedure and a function?
lessons.qsub: When should you use triggers? What problems can overusing triggers cause?
terms: Saved SQL code block — logic, params, return multiple results.
Value return karta — SELECT mein use ho sakta.
Procedure owner ki permission se run — careful.
lessons.what:
Stored Procedures = SQL+logic ka saved block, server ke paas rehta hai. Functions value (virgin scalar/tabular) return karte — SELECT my_func(x). Triggers table events par auto-fire — log, denormalization, audit yahan se.

Interview short-diff: procedure ek action/sequence; function ek value; trigger chalta hai automatic. Overusing triggers — javlan: hidden magic, jisne call kiya nahi jaanta, debugging hell.
lessons.analogy: Restaurant recipe cards (app ke paas): procedure = "andhadhundhi tray — 10 steps, dish ready" (call: CALL make_biryani). Function = "kya ye price valid hai?" (SELECT is_valid()). Trigger = ""order aate hi bill print kar do"" — tumne mat bola, system khud. Par bahut saare triggers = "ghost waiters", samajhna mushkil.
lessons.why: Interview: "procedure vs function", "triggers kyu avoid?" — Data-bound logic ka placement. Ye bhi legacy systems ke legacy code reads mein aana hota hai. Auditing/denorm through triggers = common pattern.

visual.cap: Procedure = action block; Function = returns value; Trigger = auto-fire on event.

lessons.name: Table partitioning — Range, List, Hash
lessons.desc: Partitioning splits a huge table into smaller pieces while it looks like one table. Range by date, List by discrete values, Hash for even distribution. Partition pruning skips irrelevant partitions.
lessons.q: What is partition pruning? How does it improve query performance?
lessons.qsub: When would you drop a partition instead of using DELETE? What are the trade-offs?
terms: Badi table ko chhote physical pieces mein todna — logically ek table.
Hash se distribute — even spread, range queries suffer.
Optimizer sirf relevant partitions par jaata — fast, less I/O.
lessons.what:
Partitioning ek bade table ko chhote physical segments mein todta hai (combined logical ek table banti). Types: Range (date bins), List (discrete values), Hash (even spread).

Partition pruning magic: query sirf usi partition ko scan karta jo zaroori hai — WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01' → kaafi partitions skip. Old data drop: DROP PARTITION delete ke bajaye (columns full-table hit nahi). Retention + performance dono.
lessons.analogy: Museum ke saal-bahaar store rooms: poora museum ek hai (logical), par 2024 ka saaman 2024 ke room mein (partition). "2024 ke items dikhao" = sirf ek room kholo (pruning). Purana saaman hatana = whole museum empty karna nahi, sirf ek room ka door band (DROP PARTITION).
lessons.why: Interview: at-scale tables — partition + pruning. "Logs optimize?" Range partition (dates) — common answer. Drop partition vs DELETE (no transaction issues, bloat-less). Big-table maintenance ka practical jawaab.

lessons.name: Full-text search — inverted indexes
lessons.desc: Full-text search finds words inside text much smarter than LIKE. Uses inverted index: for each word, stores list of documents containing it. Handles stemming, stop words, and relevance ranking.
lessons.q: How does an inverted index power full-text search?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between tsvector and tsquery in PostgreSQL full-text search?
terms: Word → list of documents — LIKE vice versa.
PostgreSQL: text ka processed vector (stemmed, tokens).
Search query object — @<> symbols se combine.
lessons.what:
Full-text search mere LIKE '%word%' se samajhdaar hai. Core: inverted index — har word ke liye us documents ki list jisme wo aata (book index utha ke).

PostgreSQL mein: to_tsvector text ko tokens + stemming + stop words filter karke nikalta hai; to_tsquery search banata; @@ se match; ts_rank se relevance sort. LIKE ka inverted %xyz% index use hi nahi — table scan.
lessons.analogy: Bhavya dictionary reverse: LIKE = "har panne mein ye word dhundho" (Slow). FTS = "word → jis jis page mein" mishran card — turai pehli baar word dikhao jahan kahan (inverted). Aaj ke search boxes yahi engine chalate — stemming ke saath "dogs" → "dog".
lessons.why: Search-text queries — products, blog, logs — FTS answer. LIKE wildcard-start = slow. Interview: "how do full-text indexes work?" → inverted index, stemming. Feature-matrix simple.

lessons.name: Pivot / Unpivot — row-to-column conversion
lessons.desc: PIVOT rotates rows into columns — like rotating a table 90 degrees. Most databases use CASE WHEN instead of native PIVOT. ROLLUP adds subtotals. CUBE adds subtotals for all combinations.
lessons.q: How do you pivot rows into columns using CASE WHEN?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between ROLLUP and CUBE? When would you use each?
terms: Rows ko columns mein ghuma — 90 degree rotate.
PIVOT ka manual tarika — column per condition.
lessons.what:
PIVOT table ko 90° ghuma deta hai — rows ke values columns bante. MySQL — T-SQL/Oracle native PIVOT; PostgreSQL jaisi DB mein CASE WHEN + GROUP BY se banate.

ROLLUP — child-total hierarchy: dept subtotals + overall total. CUBE — ALL combinations. Ye reporting ke liye: "sale by month, by region, by month×region". GROUPING SETS (manual list) zyada control deta.
lessons.analogy: Table of timings: har row ek class+slot. PIVOT = har slot column bana do — Monday row mein "Math, Eng...". ROLLUP = college-wise total + pura rank; CUBE = college, course, slot — hum combinations bhi. Manual CASE WHEN = "jo slot=san, usse column san mein".
lessons.why: Crosstab/reporting interview mein pivot pattern poochhte. CASE-WHEN = portable answer (jawan DB vendor). Multi-aggregate (subtotals) — ROLLUP jaise extra. Easy pointer: rotated matrix = PIVOT.

lessons.name: Normalization — 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF
lessons.desc: Normalization eliminates data redundancy. 1NF: atomic values. 2NF: no partial dependencies. 3NF: no transitive dependencies. BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key. Most production DBs normalize to 3NF.
lessons.q: What are 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF? Give an example of violating each.
lessons.qsub: What is a transitive dependency? How does 3NF eliminate it?
terms: Atomic values — har column ek hi value; break repeated groups.
No partial dependency — non-key column ko saare key ke saath depend hona.
No transitive dependency — non-key → non-key nahi.
Duplicate data — update anomalies ki jad.
lessons.what:
Normalization data ko redundancy se bachata — baar-baar same value nahi, jab update karo to ek jagah se ho. Grades: 1NF: atomic cells (list ko alag rows). 2NF: partial dependency hatao (composite key ke ek part par koi column depend na kare). 3NF: transitive — city → zip (zip se city bata di) jab non-key aise depend kare, alag table. BCNF: strict 3NF.

Production mostly 3NF normalize. Redundancy hatne se update anomalies (dobara update bhoolna) vanish.
lessons.analogy: Student aur course list: ek cell mein "Math, Eng" — 1NF todi (tod ke rows). Agar student_id (1,2) composite hai aur "student_name" sirf id-1 se depend (partial) — 2NF todi. Agar course_id → teacher_name → dept (transitive) — 3NF todi. Tables alag; clean.
lessons.why: Interview core: "explain 1NF/2NF/3NF with example". Ye schema design ka pahla quality gate. BCNF = jaano (2NF/3NF yaad rakhna). "Why normalize?" → redundancy + anomalies.

lessons.name: Denormalization — pre-joined tables, cached aggregates
lessons.desc: Denormalization intentionally adds redundancy for speed. Instead of JOINing 3 tables on every load, copy data into one table. Trade: faster reads but more complex updates and data inconsistency risk.
lessons.q: When should you denormalize a database schema?
lessons.qsub: What are the risks of denormalization? How do materialized views provide controlled denormalization?
terms: Jaandi redundancy — reads tez karne ke liye JOINs kam.
JOIN ka result pehle se store — query mein JOIN nahi.
SUM/COUNT pehle se board par — har query par recompute nahi.
Duplicate copy purani ho jaye — sync chahiye.
lessons.what:
Denormalization jaan-boojh kar redundancy se speed lena. 3NF normalized mein har read 3-4 JOIN; denormalized mein ek hi table — read fast, par writes mein consistency का ध्यान.

lessons.why: Interview: "when denormalize?" — read-heavy hot paths में. Ye bhi sahi jawaab hai isliye ki saare JOINs slow na ho translation memo. Materialized view se controlled rehta hai — production best practice.

lessons.qsub: What is the difference between a strong entity and a weak entity?

Entities ke beech ka rishta — line + cardinality.
Apne parent ke bina exist nahi — e.g. order items.
lessons.what:
ER diagram SQL se pehle ka blueprint. Entities = cheezein (tables), attributes = columns, relationships + cardinality = rishta ka hisab (1:1, 1:N, M:N).

lessons.name: Schema patterns — STI, CTI; Embedding vs Referencing
lessons.desc: Single Table Inheritance puts all types in one table with nullable columns. Class Table Inheritance uses base + type-specific tables. In NoSQL: Embedding stores data inside the document, Referencing stores IDs.
lessons.q: When would you use embedding vs referencing in MongoDB?
lessons.qsub: What are the trade-offs between Single Table Inheritance and Class Table Inheritance?
terms: Single Table Inheritance — ek table, types nullable columns se.
Class Table Inheritance — base table + type-specific tables + FK.
NoSQL (Mongo): data andar hi — no JOIN.
Ek concept, kai shapes — modelling choice.
lessons.what:
STI ek table mein saare types (user + admin same table, un-used columns NULL). Simple, fast reads, par null-heavy + widening schema. CTI — base table sab common columns; subclasses alag table FK ke sath. Clean, par JOIN hamesha.

NoSQL mein: embedding related data andar rakhna (address inside user) — reads single query; referencing — sirf ids, alag collection. Embed for 1:1/1:few & read-together; reference for many/independent.
lessons.analogy: Office register: STI = ek register — har type ke apne khali khane (NULL) bharne; CTI = base register (nam) + type-specific diaries (salary, projects) se jod ke. NoSQL: embedding = "address card user ki file mein stapled", referencing = "address card alag almari, file mein uska number".
lessons.why: Schema patterns production me every modeling decision. STI vs CTI — Rails-type legacy; Embed vs Reference — Mongo interview favourite. "When embed when reference?" — high-signal answer.

lessons.name: Star Schema & Snowflake Schema
lessons.desc: Star schema: central fact table (metrics) surrounded by dimension tables (attributes). Snowflake normalizes dimensions. Star is preferred for query performance. Fact tables are deep and narrow.
lessons.q: What is the difference between a star schema and a snowflake schema?
lessons.qsub: What is a slowly changing dimension? How do Type 1 and Type 2 handle changes over time?
terms: Center — numeric measures (sales amount), deep, many rows.
Fact + flattened dims — single join level, fast.
Dims normalized further — less redundancy, more joins.
SCD: dims badalte (address). Type1 overwrite, Type2 version rows.
lessons.what:
Star schema analytics ka standard: beech mein fact table (measures, miloonse numbers) + chodon dimension tables denormalized (dates, products). Har fact dim ki foreign keys. Snowflake dimensions ko bhi 2NF normalize — redundancy kam, par joins zyada.

Star fast (flat, direct joins) isliye preferred. Slowly Changing Dimensions: jab dimension badle (customer location), Type 1 = overwrite (simple, history lost), Type 2 = naye version row (history preserved).
lessons.analogy: Ganit ki map: fact = "kitna becha" numbers (center). Dimensions = "kab (date), kya (product), kahan (store)" — un codes (axis). Star: har axis ek line se, no nested maze. Snowflake: axes further sub-limes hinne ONg (more pieces). SCD: customer ka city badla — type1 = overwrite (mazboot), type2 = nai lineage row add.
lessons.why: Analytics/interview: "design sales warehouse" — star schema evaluation. SCD2 ka answer us post ke embedding questions ko todta. "Star vs snowflake" — perf vs flexibility.

lessons.name: ACID properties — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
lessons.desc: ACID guarantees reliable transactions. Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: valid state transitions. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere. Durability: committed data survives crashes.
lessons.q: Explain each ACID property with a real-world example.
lessons.qsub: How is atomicity implemented in PostgreSQL? What role does the write-ahead log play?
terms: All-or-nothing — transaction ka andar koi state nahi.
DB rules ke mutabik valid state — constraints hold.
Concurrent transactions ek doosre se interference na karein.
Commit ke baad data pakka — crash par bhi.
Write-Ahead Log — pehle log, phir data; recovery ka adhar.
lessons.what:
ACID transaction ki guarantee: Atomicity — 200 jaye 100 DOB, dono ya koi nahi. Consistency — transaction ke baad bhi constraints (A to z FK/check) valid. Isolation — saath saath chalane par bhi result jaise alag-alaag chale. Durability — commit bol diya to crash ke baad bhi data dikh raha.

PG mein atomicity/durability WAL se: har change pehle log (organized write) mein, phir data page. Crash par WAL se redo — kuch lost nahi.
lessons.analogy: Gift transfer (A se B ko 100): Atomicity = dono jagah credit-debit perfect yaa zero. Consistency = poori dukaan ke rules (balance >= 0) toote nahi. Isolation = do khaat ekatthe update bhi ek-dam ke hisaab se. Durability = receipt bana (WAL) — dukaan ki light gayi to bhi dobara ₹100 wapas-credit kar paoge.
lessons.why: ACID interview foundation — har transaction/concurrency question yahan se banta. "Consistency vs Isolation", "WAL kya" — core DB internals. Ye bhi explain karta hai why full-DB transactions over files.

lessons.name: Isolation levels — Read Committed to Serializable
lessons.desc: Isolation levels control how much one transaction can see of others work. READ COMMITTED (default), REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. Higher isolation reduces anomalies but reduces concurrency.
lessons.q: What is the difference between READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ?
lessons.qsub: What anomalies can occur at each isolation level? How does Snapshot Isolation work?
terms: Kitna doosra transaction dikh raha — 4 levels.
PG default — sirf committed data, har statement apna snapshot.
Transaction ke start ka snapshot — baar-baar same result.
Jaise serial chala — highest bar, sab anomalies blocked.
Dirty read, non-repeatable, phantom — levels inhe kontrol karte.
lessons.what:
Isolation levels decide karte ki ek transaction doosre ka kaam kitna dekhega. 4 levels: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads allowed), READ COMMITTED (dirty nahi — PG default), REPEATABLE READ (snapshot — same query same answer), SERIALIZABLE (jaise sab serial).

Anomalies: dirty read (uncommitted data dekhna), non-repeatable read (dusri baar query alag answer), phantom (nayi rows nazar aagayi). Zyada isolation = safer, kam concurrency. PG MVCC se REPEATABLE READ cheap milta.
lessons.analogy: Exam hall copies: READ COMMITTED = har question par turant latest ink (dusri baar question ka answer badal sakta). REPEATABLE READ = gate ke samay ka paper copy (4 ghante same copy). SERIALIZABLE = ek baar mein ek banda paper deta, baaki wait — safest, slowest. Dirty read = rukta hua ink padhna — dark.
lessons.why: Interview: "which isolation level? Read Committed default kyun?" — PG ki REPEATABLE READ se phantoms control. Concurrency + consistency ka dial — core OLTP knowledge. Read/write bugs yahi se samajh aate.

lessons.name: MVCC — Multi-Version Concurrency Control
lessons.desc: MVCC keeps multiple versions of each row so readers and writers never block each other. Readers see old versions, writers create new ones. Postgres uses xmin/xmax columns. VACUUM cleans old versions.
lessons.q: How does MVCC allow readers and writers to work simultaneously?
lessons.qsub: What are xmin and xmax in PostgreSQL? What happens if vacuum does not run?
terms: Multi-Version Concurrency Control — har row ke kai versions.
Row kis transaction ne banaya — visibility.
ROW kisne delete/update kiya — version store.
Transaction ko ek point-in-time view milta.
Old versions ki safai — bloat control.
lessons.what:
MVCC PostgreSQL ka secret: har row ke multiple versions rehte. Writer naya version banata, readers apne snapshot ke mutabik purana dekhte — isliye reader aur writer block nahi hote.

PG rows par xmin (kaunsi transaction ne banaya) aur xmax (kaunsi ne delete/update kiya) hota — snapshot rules in se decide karte ki kaunsa version dikhana. Purane versions tab tak pade rehte jab tak VACUUM unhe saf kare — vacuum na chale to bloat (storage na badhta table slow).
lessons.analogy: Homework notebook ke carbon copies: har update par nayi blank copy banti (new version). Teacher (reader) ko apni class starting ka copy pakda hua hai — tab tak padh sakte jab tak class ka naya copy. Copy board par (xmin/xmax) batate kaunsa version kisne pakda. Roje suraj nikalne par purani copy jalao (VACUUM) — warna room bhar jaayega.
lessons.why: Interview concurrency heart: "how do PG reads/writes not block?" → MVCC. xmin/xmax, snapshot isolation, vacuum. Ye bhi PG vs row-lock DBs ka fundamental improvement dikhata.

lessons.name: Locking — row-level, intent locks, deadlocks
lessons.desc: Shared locks allow multiple readers but block writers. Exclusive locks block everyone. Deadlock occurs when transactions wait for each other in a cycle. Database detects and kills one transaction.
lessons.q: What is the difference between shared and exclusive locks? When is each used?
lessons.qsub: How does a database detect deadlocks? What is the wait-for graph?
terms: Read lock — kai readers allowed, writer blocks.
Write lock — sirf ek, baaki sab block.
A transaction B ka wait, B A ka wait — cycle.
Deadlock detection: kaun kis lipra hai.
Table-level hint — row locks honi wali hain.
lessons.what:
Locks concurrency kontrol karte: shared (READ — kai ek saath, koi writer nahi), exclusive (WRITE — ek banda, baaki wait). Intent locks table-level signal dete ki row par locks aane wale hain.

Deadlock tab jab A ke paas row1, B ke paas row2; A cancel row2, B row1 — dono wait. DB wait-for graph banakar cycle pakadta aur ek victim ko rollback karta (convert ukkaisi ke pasand ki round).
lessons.analogy: Ek-paper-to-devan book: shared = kai padh sakte (lekin koi change nahi). Exclusive = koi likh raha — kahin aur le lo line. Deadlock = student A kaha le lo B wali, B le lo A wali — dono atke. Teacher (DB) cycle dekhte hi "A tu chhod" (rollback) — uska paper agle sapna.
lessons.why: Interview gorvesh concurrency: row vs table lock, deadlock cycle + detection, victim rollback crystal. "Why deadlock and how to avoid" — lock ordering mantri shastra.

lessons.name: Distributed transactions — 2PC, 3PC, Saga pattern
lessons.desc: Two-Phase Commit coordinates distributed transactions: prepare phase then commit phase. Problem: coordinator crash blocks everyone. Saga pattern fixes this with local transactions and compensating actions.
lessons.q: What is the problem with Two-Phase Commit? How does the Saga pattern address it?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between choreography-based and orchestration-based sagas?
terms: Prepare + pre-commit + commit — coordinator crash recovery better.
Local transactions + compensating actions — no global lock.
Saga events se — messages, no central coordinator.
lessons.what:
Distributed transactions kai services/nodes ke beech — ab global commit karna. 2PC: phase1 prepare (sab "ready"), phase2 commit — agar koi fail, sab abort. Problem: coordinator crash par sab atke (blocking). 3PC extra pre-commit se crash recovery better, par network-partition par still not perfect.

Saga pattern modern answer: global transaction nahi — local transactions sequence + compensating actions (kalyan rollback). Choreography = events se flow; orchestration = controller se.
lessons.analogy: Group picnic plan: 2PC = har banda call par "ho sakta hoon" (prepare), phir sab confirm (commit). Ek nahi ho wanna jisko — sab koi ja nahi (rollback). Agar coordinator bhoolh jaye — cricket standstill. Saga = khud turant plan (step-by-step); agar koi step fail, agli steps ko "wapas cancel" karke fix (compensate) — koi global rule nahi.
lessons.why: Microservices interview ka pressure topic. 2PC blocking flaw + saga compensating fix — clear contrast. "2PC vs saga when" — financial consistency vs availability.

lessons.name: CAP Theorem — Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance
lessons.desc: CAP theorem: a distributed system can only guarantee 2 of 3 properties. Since partitions are unavoidable, you choose CP (consistent, may refuse requests) or AP (available, may return stale data).
lessons.q: Explain the CAP theorem. What is the difference between CP and AP systems?
lessons.qsub: What is PACELC? How does it extend CAP with latency/consistency trade-offs in normal operation?
terms: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance — tin mein se do.
Har read latest write dekhe hai.
Har request answer mein jab node up.
Network cut ke beech bhi chalta rahe.
CP = consistency deta (requests reject); AP = availability (stale chalta).
lessons.what:
CAP theorem: distributed system do hi guarantees pakki kar sakta jab network partition ho — Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance. Partition unavoidable hai (network tootenge), isliye choice: CP (Zab, Mongo) — consistent par downtime/kam availability, ya AP (Cassandra, DynamoDB) — available par stale data.

Normal time mein sab 3 theek — CAP ka tension sirf partition ke time. PACELC extend: partition bina — latency vs consistency trade.
lessons.analogy: Two shops, ek highway baandh: partition = phone line door. CP = "bina aakhari rate pehchane, bechnay nahi" (safe, koi nahi chalti) — consistent par closed. AP = "jo value pata hai usi se behn" (shop khuli, rate purana ho sakta). Highway wapas khule to rates jod lo.
lessons.why: NoSQL interview ka opening frame — "why consistency trade-offs?" Ye base hai; every distributed store isko mention karta. CAP ko example wale answers mein rank karo — wahi signal.

lessons.name: BASE vs ACID — consistency trade-offs
lessons.desc: BASE is the NoSQL consistency model: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually Consistent. The opposite of ACID. System always responds, data may be temporarily inconsistent, eventually all replicas converge.
lessons.q: What is BASE? How does it differ from ACID?
lessons.qsub: When is eventual consistency acceptable? Give examples where it is not.
terms: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually Consistent — NoSQL.
Copy ka data age badal sakta (no fixed state).
Dino ke baad sab copies equal ho jayengi.
lessons.what:
BASE ACID ka NoSQL counterpart — ACID nahi aur availability + scale. Basically Available: har request answer. Soft state: replicas ka data continuously update ho sakta. Eventually consistent: kuch der puraani, magar aakhri mein sab replicas same.

Use kab: leaderboards, likes, cache, follower feeds — jahan thodi der purana data chalega. NOT: money, inventory — wahan ACID chahiye.
lessons.analogy: Whatsapp status baantna: likho to turant tumhare phone pe. Dosto ke phone par thodi der baad (eventually) dikhega. Garantised koi exact state nahi (soft state) — bas system rehta hai. Iske ult currency transfer = ACID — turant, exact, sahi.
lessons.why: Interview "BASE vs ACID" — NoSQL consistency lingo. Apologies "when is eventual OK" the approval-savvy answer. Ye bhi CAP ke AP side ko concrete banata.

lessons.name: Key-Value stores — Redis, DynamoDB
lessons.desc: Key-value stores are the simplest NoSQL model: key maps to value. Redis stores everything in RAM for sub-millisecond speed. Supports data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets. TTL for auto-expiry.
lessons.q: What are the use cases for Redis? When would you choose it over a relational database?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between Redis persistence options RDB and AOF?

RAM mein — sub-ms; strings, lists, sets, sorted sets.
AWS managed — KV + docs, replica scale.
Redis: RDB snapshot + AOF append log.
lessons.what:
Key-Value store sabse seedha model — key par value, O(1) get/set. Redis: sab RAM mein — sub-millisecond, data structures (string, hash, list, set, sorted set), TTL expiry, aur persistence options RDB (point-in-time snapshot) vs AOF (append-only log, granular). DynamoDB — AWS managed, partiioned replicated, auto-scaling.

Consistency config: Redis single-threaded strong-mur; DynamoDB eventual default (strong optional). Rank hamesha caching/session/rate-limit mein.
lessons.analogy: Chhota sa pocket diary yaadgaar: kanah number → naam turant (O(1)). Redis = diary RAM mein — diary bhi band karne par kuch copy chahiye: RDB = photo copy (pura snapshot), AOF = note-by-note addon log (har change record). TTL = "kaal subah is page ko bhool jana" (automatic expiry).

lessons.name: Document stores — MongoDB, Firestore
lessons.desc: Document stores save JSON-like documents where each can have different structure. Great for flexible schemas. MongoDB organizes documents into collections. Embedding related data inside documents avoids JOINs.
lessons.q: When would you choose MongoDB over PostgreSQL?
lessons.qsub: What is the 16MB document limit in MongoDB? How does it affect schema design?
terms: JSON-like docs — har doc alag structure. MongoDB, Firestore.
Related data doc ke andar — JOIN nahi.
Dusre doc ke id — lookup karna.
MongoDB single doc ki max limit.
lessons.what:
Document stores JSON-ish documents save karte hain — har document ki structure flexible. MongoDB: collections (tables), aur embedding (related data andar) se JOINs nahi karne padte. Firestore similar — realtime sync ke liye popular.

Trade: flexible schema quicks eh flexible reads ko predict karna mushkil. MongoDB limited docs — 16MB — isliye embedding greedy list = chhota dikhna chahiye. Relationships doosre thor: embeds (1:few) vs references (many/independent).
lessons.analogy: Form sab malik ki file: har user ki ek file, saara user-internal data (address, phone) andar nahi (embed) — dono fee look karo, koi merge (JOIN) nahi. Agar orders bade list ho to file khatam (16MB) — unke compounds (dosto mein) separate register (referencing). File to grid alag hogi — to hi grid faltu/data hai.
lessons.why: Interview: "Mongo vs Postgres kyon?" — flexible schema + scale + no JOIN cost vs consistency & joins. Embed vs reference = schema philosophy. Document stores yahan se product-search, profiles, catalog.

lessons.name: Column-Family stores — Cassandra, HBase
lessons.desc: Column-family stores distribute data across nodes using consistent hashing. No single point of failure. Design tables around queries, not data models. No JOINs — create separate tables for each access pattern.
lessons.q: Why does Cassandra require query-first data modeling?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between a partition key and a clustering key in Cassandra?
terms: Row key + sorted columns groups — Cassandra, HBase.
Kis node par data jaaega (consistent hash).
Pehle queries, phir tables — No JOINs.
Node add/remove par kam data move — Cassandra.
lessons.what:
Column-family stores (Cassandra, HBase) data ko row key + sorted columns mein rakhte aur consistent hashing se nodes par distribute karte — no single point of failure.

Rule: design tables around queries, not data. No JOINs — har access pattern ke liye uski table (denormalized). Partition key decide karta node; clustering key partition ke andar order. Queries ko apne partition key se filter karna hoga — warna full cluster scan.

lessons.why: Cassandra architecture interview — no single point, query-first data model, partition app clustering. Ye distributed write scale ka king hai. "Design a write-heavy system" — Cassandra surfacing.

lessons.name: Graph databases — Neo4j, Cypher
lessons.desc: Graph databases store nodes (things) and edges (relationships). Perfect when relationships are as important as data — social networks, fraud detection, recommendations. Cypher query language uses ASCII art syntax.
lessons.q: When would you choose a graph database over a relational database?
lessons.qsub: How does traversal depth affect performance in a graph database?
terms: Relationship follow karke khol dhoondhna — depth matters.
lessons.what:
Graph databases relationships ko first-class citizen banate. Nodes + directed labelled edges. Jaise relationships hi data ho — social graph, fraud rings, recommendations. Cypher = ASCII-art SQL: MATCH (a)-[:FRIEND]->(b) — (persons) -relation- (persons).

Relational mein 6-JOIN friendship depth = brutal; graph mein traversal natural. Par traversal depth ke saath count explode — ye graph ka hidden cost.
lessons.analogy: Wedding cat: friends ki photo line + "ye do patni wale hain" tape (edges). "Sam ke dost ke dost ke dost kaun?" — line follow karte chalo (traverse). Relational = har jagah joining register ka hi chepna (JOINs); graph = dekh kar chhodne wali. Par jitna door jaoge (depth), utni bheed bhi badhegi.
lessons.why: Interview: "relational vs graph kyon?" — relationship-heavy depth queries. Fraud (2-hop accounts), recommends, social — graph jaadu dikhata. Cypher reading ek plus.

lessons.name: Time-series databases — InfluxDB, TimescaleDB
lessons.desc: Time-series databases optimize for append-heavy, time-ordered data like metrics and sensor readings. TimescaleDB extends PostgreSQL with automatic time-based partitioning. Append-only, never updates past readings.
lessons.q: What makes a time-series database different from a regular database?
lessons.qsub: What is downsampling and why is it essential for long-term metric retention?
terms: Time-stamped data — append heavy, never update. InfluxDB, TimescaleDB.
Old data ka coarse aggregation — storage kam.
lessons.what:
Time-series databases metrics/sensors ke liye: data append-only, hamesha time-prefixed, past update nahi. TimescaleDB = PostgreSQL + time partitioning (hypertables) — SQL hi rehta. InfluxDB — purpose-built, TSM compression + downsampling.

Downsampling: 1-minute raw kuch mahine baad 1-hour avg — retention byt lines. Ye long-term storage ko light. Regular DB time-range joins par struggle; TS DB time-order I/O optimize karta.
lessons.analogy: Weather station ki diary: har minute temperature likhna (append). Kabhi purana entry nahi sudharna (append-only). Saal bhar ka 1-min data bhaari — isliye mahine bhar baad hourly average khol do (downsample), 10 saal baad delete (retention). Normal DB diary mein to page pura padhne padta; TS DB entry column mujhe turant date ke hisaab se milega.
lessons.why: Interview: "monitoring/observability daa kahan rakhein?" — TSDB. Downsampling + retention = scaling storage sanwaad. Timescale = PG + TS eco. Real-world system design (metrics pipeline).

lessons.name: Sharding — hash, range, consistent hashing
lessons.desc: Sharding splits data across multiple servers. Hash sharding distributes evenly. Range sharding enables range queries but risks hot spots. Cross-shard JOINs are expensive or impossible.
lessons.q: What is the difference between hash sharding and range sharding?
lessons.qsub: What is consistent hashing? How does it minimize data movement when nodes join or leave?
terms: Data ko kai servers mein baant — horizontal scale.
key_hash % N — even spread, range queries suffer.
Key range ke hisaab — range scan okay, hot spots.
Node add/remove par sirf kam keys move hoti.
lessons.what:
Sharding ek table ka data kai nodes par divide — jab ek node boostrap nahi kar sakta. Hash sharding: key ke hash se node pehle — distribution even, par range queries ko saare nodes chahiye. Range sharding: date/user-id bins — range query tez, par ek "hot" bin saara traffic khayega.

Consistent hashing: nodes ko circle par rakho; node hatne par use sab saath poocha jata nahi — sirf chhota segment. Re-sharding/scaling = jhanjhat; isliye buckets + virtual nodes.
lessons.analogy: Bada library kai shelves: hash = book ke title ka hash decide poster "sheld 3" — even filling, par "authors A-K" (range) dhundhne sab shelves chahiye. Range = A-K shelf aap uthe — author dhundhna asaan par "Z" me itni kahline sab ki di (hot). Consistent ring = adding shelf par sabse door? sirf 1-2 kahliya hailo, baaki reh jaati apni jagah.
lessons.why: System-design interview "scale the DB" — sharding ka pahla jawaab. Hash vs range + hot spot + rebalancing cost. Cross-shard JOIN/ACID limits bhi batana = senior level.

lessons.name: Replication — single-leader, multi-leader, leaderless
lessons.desc: Replication copies data across nodes for fault tolerance and read scaling. Single-leader: one writes, followers copy. Multi-leader: multiple accept writes. Leaderless: any node accepts writes with quorum.
lessons.q: What is the difference between single-leader and multi-leader replication?
lessons.qsub: How does leaderless replication handle conflict resolution? What are CRDTs?
terms: Ek writer (leader), replicas copy — reads scale.
Do writes same key — LWW, CRDT, vector clocks.
lessons.what:
Replication data ki copies nodes par — fault tolerance + read scale. Single-leader: ek leader writes, followers replay (async/sync). Reads followers par (but lag → stale). Multi-leader: kai writers — conflict resolution zaroori (LWW, CRDT). Leaderless: koi bhi node writes, quorum (W+R > N) se read guaranteed fresh — DynamoDB style.

Replication lag se read-your-write, monotonic reads — experience. Async = fast but data loss risk on leader crash.
lessons.analogy: Ghar ka notepad + copies: father likhta (leader), ghar ke juniors copies banate (replicas). Reading copies faster par chota sa bath rook les (lag). Multi-leader = dono parents likhte — "bhatiya pics" dobara dono jagah — kaunsi prefer? (conflict: jo aakhri time, ya bhej dono merge — CRDT). Leaderless = sab bhaag ke likhte; quorum: 3 loge padho, 2 ne likhna zaroor = latest milega.
lessons.why: Interview: replication (leader modes) + lag issues + conflict handling — distributed DB debate ka core. "Why replica lag matters" product-level. Quorum math = engineer reasoning.

lessons.name: Consensus — Raft, Paxos
lessons.desc: Consensus algorithms ensure multiple nodes agree on a value despite failures. Raft: elect leader, leader handles writes, majority must acknowledge. If leader crashes, followers elect a new one.
lessons.q: How does Raft leader election work? What happens when the leader crashes?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between Raft and Paxos? Why is Raft preferred for implementability?
terms: Nodes ek hi value par agree — even with failures.
Older consensus — correct but hard to implement.
lessons.what:
Consensus algorithms (Raft, Paxos) multiple nodes ko ek hi state par keep karte hain failures ke bawajood. Raft: leader elected (terms, votes, majority), leader writes ko log mein, majority ack se commit. Leader crash → timeout → new election.

Majority rule split-brain rokta: ek time par ek hi leader. Paxos: correct par sikhna/implement karna andher; isliye Raft practical favorite. Use: etcd, ZooKeeper, CockroachDB replication, Kafka controller.
lessons.analogy: Panchayat voting: mukhiya election (term → votes → majority). Mukhiya ka order sab parchment par likhte (log). Jab majority "pakda" (commit) — turant. Mukhiya door — naya chunav (new term). Do mukhiya? nahi — 5 mein 3 votes majority hi ek ko mandate. Raft = aasan process; Paxos = mathematical siddha but implement karna buddhi (rare).
lessons.why: Interview: "how do distributed nodes agree?" — leader election, majority, split-brain. Raft easy narrative — terms/timeouts/logs. ye distributed consistency ka base hai (ZAB, etcd).

lessons.name: Gossip protocol — peer-to-peer state dissemination
lessons.desc: Gossip spreads information without a central coordinator. Each node periodically picks a random neighbor and shares state. After O(log N) rounds, all nodes know. Used by Cassandra for cluster membership.
lessons.q: How does the gossip protocol spread information across a cluster?
lessons.qsub: What is the Phi Accrual failure detector? How does Cassandra use it?
terms: Node random saathi ko state batata — O(log N) rounds me sab ko.
No central coordinator — har node barabar.
Failure detector — heartbeat gap se suspicion level.
Cluster kaunse nodes live — gossip se maintain.
Sab nodes ka ek hi view — rounds ke baad.
lessons.what:
Gossip protocol — rumour failne jaise: har node baar-baar random neighbor ko state bhejta hai. Ek hi source waste nahi — O(log N) rounds sab ko pata chal jaata. Cassandra/DynamoDB cluster membership yahan se (kaun live), bina central list.

Scalable + self-healing (koi single point nahi). Phi Accrual failure detector heartbeat samay ke gap se "kya ye node mar gaya?" probability — fixed timeout se behtar.
lessons.analogy: Ganv ka shor: ek khabar seedha sab ko nahi — har banda apne 2-3 padosi ko bolta. Har goonji ke saath naye log milte jaate. 10 baar mein poore gaon ko patta. Agar koi ghar se reply nahi — padosi bolte "nauishan raha hai tanak" (suspicion), pukka timing gap se (phi). Koi takat ka center nahi — sab share kar rahe.
lessons.why: Interview: "distributed membership bina coordinator?" — gossip. Cassandra failure detector — production gossip. Ye cluster self-management ke internals dikhata. "How does a node know cluster is changing?" — rounds.

lessons.name: CQRS — separate read/write models
lessons.desc: CQRS separates write model (normalized, transactional) from read model (pre-computed, optimized). Scale reads and writes independently. Write to Postgres, read from Redis or Elasticsearch.
lessons.q: What problem does CQRS solve? When should you NOT use it?
lessons.qsub: How do you keep the read model in sync with the write model? What consistency guarantees does it provide?
terms: Simple CRUD apps — complexity justify nahi.
lessons.what:
CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) write aur read ke alag models. Write: normalized/txn-safe (Postgres). Read: optimized shapes (Redis/Elasticsearch precomputed). Scale dono alag — reads zyada, writes mhnwr alag.

Sync read model events se (jaise CDC deeb, outbox) — poore app ko ye eventually consistent. Zaroori? nahi — simple crud par overhead. Tab use jab reads/writes asymmetric + hot queries need denormalization.
lessons.analogy: Book: hardcover bolne waale ek (writer) aur liuqh books jaan karne waale (reader). Writer register mein sab. Readers ko readers-format cards — har ek view (dashboardA) ka apna proj. Bina reporter log, loudly. Aaj kaapp — event se card update. Simple app: writer & reader ke liye same hi book rakhne mein bada long.
lessons.why: Interview: "scale reads vs writes differently" — CQRS ka jawab. Ledger → reporting mein asli use. Ye event-driven arch + eventual consistency ka yokta karta. Aur "when NOT to use CQRS" — judgment.
