lessons.name: Event Sourcing — append-only event log
lessons.desc: Event Sourcing stores every state change as an immutable event instead of current state. Current state is derived by replaying events. Gives complete audit trail and time travel debugging.
lessons.q: What is the difference between Event Sourcing and traditional CRUD storage?
lessons.qsub: What are projections in event sourcing? How do snapshots improve replay performance?
terms: State nahi, events store — har change append-only log.
Past fact — immutable, kabhi change nahi.
Events se current state nikalna — read model.
Replay short karna — periodic state save.
lessons.what:
Event sourcing current state nahi, balki har state change ko event store karta hai (append-only). Balance 500 ka matlab "OPENED(100), DEPOSIT(200), WITHDRAW(?)" — poora itihas. Current state replay (projection) se.

Faayda: full audit trail + time travel. Piche jab encryption ki — ab state change ho gayi. Kam: events kabhi update nahi, schema bhi evolve tricky, replay slow → snapshots periodic milestone. Traditional CRUD overwrite karta; ES sirf append.
lessons.analogy: Bank passbook (aajka app): balance upar-hot na number nahi, para har transaction likha (DEPOSIT +200, WITHDRAW -50). Har page ek event — kabhi mitao nahi. "Balance kya?" = sab entries ka sum (projection). Bahut zaada pages → har 50 page par summary (snapshot) — aage se usse count. App review chahe — tamam itihas maujood.
lessons.why: Event-driven arch + audit + rebuildable state — interview rich: ES vs CRUD, projections, snapshots. Ye bhi CQRS ke saath jada pairs. "Time travel debugging" — senior signal.

lessons.name: CDC — Change Data Capture, Debezium
lessons.desc: CDC streams every database change to other systems in real-time by reading the transaction log. No application code changes needed. Debezium reads PostgreSQL WAL and sends events to Kafka.
lessons.q: How does log-based CDC work? Why is it better than trigger-based CDC?
lessons.qsub: What is the dual-write problem and how does CDC solve it?
terms: Change Data Capture — DB changes ko realtime stream.
Tool: PG WAL padh kar Kafka ko events bhejta.
App ne DB + Kafka alag-alag likha — inconsistency.
DB mein hi event table — reliable source.
lessons.what:
CDC database ki changes ko realtime stream banata — bin/wal log padhke (insert/update/delete). Koi app code change nahi. Debezium PG/MySQL ka WAL walta hai — events Kafka mein.

Problem solve: dual-write (app → DB + app → Kafka) mein "DB hua, Kafka fail" wala gap. CDC log se hota — bina gap, reliable. Use: sync Elasticsearch, denormalized read model, data warehouse streaming, event-driven.
lessons.analogy: Vibrant diary + reader: app register mein likha (DB) — diary (journal), aur "diary reader" (Debezium) har naye line ko duosri jagah (Kafka bazaar) live shaaf kar raha — bina app ko kuch bataye. Agar app khud register + faltu copy karta to agar copy fail — register hua par copy nahi (dual-write gap). Log reader = copy hamesha source se, koi gap nahi.
lessons.why: Modern data arch: Postgres → Kafka → search/cache/lake. Interview: "keep search in sync?" — CDC. Dual-write problem ka clean answer + outbox. Ye event-driven + warehouse pattern ka bridge.

lessons.name: OLTP vs OLAP — row vs columnar storage
lessons.desc: OLTP handles day-to-day operations with fast single-row queries. OLAP handles analytics scanning millions of rows. OLTP uses row storage. OLAP uses column storage for faster scanning and compression.
lessons.q: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP workloads?
lessons.qsub: Why is columnar storage 10-100x faster for analytics than row storage?
terms: Online Transaction Processing — daily app writes/reads, row-based. Postgres/MySQL.
Online Analytical Processing — big scans, aggregations, columnar. Warehouse.
Data row-wise disk par — OLTP ki fitrat.
Data column-wise — OLAP scan sirf relevant columns.
Hybrid — dono ek system (SingleStore) ya hybrid arch.
lessons.what:
OLTP app ka daily routine — chhoti queries, simple writes (orders, cart), hamesha row keyed. OLAP analytics — lambi queries, poore columns ka scan, aggregates (reporting), columnar store se fast kyunki sirf zaroori columns padhne.

Dono alag kyun: OLTP ki need = fast writes/rows; OLAP = wide scans. Ek ki zameen par doosra nahi chalta — isliye alag stores (warehouse) ya HTAP. Trick: koi ek DB dono ki age nahi — typecast.
lessons.analogy: Kiran store vs MBA report: OLTP = kirana par har item ka bill (turant, ek customer). OLAP = quarter end: "sab customers ka average order" (poori files kholo, calculate). Kirana par sabka average nikale to customer ka wait — isliye alag "report room" (warehouse). Columnar = pehle se sirf paise ka column nikala, baakiyon ko mat chhedo.
lessons.why: Interview: "OLTP vs OLAP" — database selection ka pehla question. Row vs columnar store answer senior dikhata. Ye warehousing + analytics bench schema tak connect hota.

lessons.name: Data warehousing — Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift
lessons.desc: Data warehouses consolidate data from multiple sources for analytics. Columnar storage compresses and scans only needed columns. Snowflake separates compute from storage. BigQuery is serverless.
lessons.q: What is the difference between ELT and ETL? Why is ELT preferred for modern warehouses?
lessons.qsub: How does Snowflake separate compute from storage? What are the cost implications?
terms: Central analytics DB — multiple sources ka integrated data.
Load pehle, transform DB mein — modern (dbt).
lessons.what:
Data warehouse poore organization ki analytics hub hai — OLTP sources (orders, users) se data ETL karke clean star schema mein. ELT (modern): pehle raw load, phir SQL transformations (dbt) — flexible + scalable.

Reporting/BI queries OLTP par heavy hoti — warehouse alag engine (columnar) + schema tuned for analysis. Star schema = fact + dims. OLAP cubes/aggregation tables drill-down ko fast banate.
lessons.analogy: Alag akhbaar ka daftar: branches alag-alag bechti hain (OLTP), daftar (warehouse) shaam ko saare branches se khole (ETL): saaf karke, maapke tabulate. Kuch aaj hi bojh pahunchao, baad mein saaf karo (ELT) — dbt engineer transform. Reports clerk isi daftar se counting karta — cross-branch totals.
lessons.why: Analytics arch interview — warehouse vs OLTP, ETL vs ELT, star schema. "How analytics scale?" — warehouse answer. Ye reporting pipelines + BI tools ka center.

lessons.name: Data Lake & Lakehouse — Delta Lake, Iceberg
lessons.desc: Data lakes store raw files cheaply on object storage. Lakehouse adds ACID transactions on top. Delta Lake: Parquet + transaction log. Iceberg: partition evolution. Hudi: incremental processing.
lessons.q: What problems does a Data Lakehouse solve that a raw data lake cannot?
lessons.qsub: What is time travel in Delta Lake? How does the transaction log work?
terms: Raw files ka vast store (S3/GCS) — schema on read.
Write par juda; lake = read par define.
Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Hudi — ACID par data.
lessons.what:
Data lake raw files ka torrent — S3 par unstructured, schema on read (jo chahiye wahi define karo). Cheap + vast. Lakehouse lake ki storage + warehouse jaisi guarantees: ACID tables (Delta, Iceberg) schema enforce + time travel. Medallion bronze → silver → gold — raw se quality ka safar.

Warehouse vs lake: warehouse = curated queries; lake = raw explore + ML. Lakehouse = dono. Ye modern data platform ka default.
lessons.analogy: Ghar ka bada godown vs library: data lake = godown — saara saaman raw kiska (S3), jo chahiye use nikaal (schema on read). Par godown mein koi hisaab (ACID) nahi — cheezein kho jaayein. Lakehouse = godown + librarian register — har box catalogue (Delta table), transaction-safe, purana record bhi milta. Gold shelf = curated kitaabein.
lessons.why: Modern data platform interview — lake vs warehouse vs lakehouse. Medallion quality layers + Delta/Iceberg = baseline. "How data team organises raw data" ka senior understanding.

visual.cap: Lake = raw on S3. Lakehouse = ACID tables on lake. Medallion = Bronze→Gold.

lessons.name: NewSQL — CockroachDB, TiDB, Spanner
lessons.desc: NewSQL gives you SQL + ACID + horizontal scaling. CockroachDB: distributed SQL with Raft consensus. Spanner: globally distributed with TrueTime for external consistency. SQL interface, NoSQL scale.
lessons.q: How does CockroachDB achieve distributed ACID transactions?
lessons.qsub: What is TrueTime in Google Spanner? Why does it require atomic clocks and GPS?
terms: SQL + ACID + distributed scale — relational hi modern.
PG wire — Raft consensus, kv internals.
Google — global txns + TrueTime (2PC across DC).
Consensus — leader logs replicas, majority commit.
lessons.what:
NewSQL = SQL + ACID jo horizontally scale karta hai — NoSQL ka sacrifice nahi (Mongo ne ACID/joins chhora; NewSQL nahi). CockroachDB (PG compatible, Raft), TiDB (MySQL compatible), Spanner (Google — global distributed txns with atomic clocks).

Trade: distributed txn logic kathin; cross-region latency. In ka use jab single PG scale-up bhann na pare. NewSQL = modern relational dream: SQL, joins, ACID, internal sharding.
lessons.analogy: Bade mall ki single billing: normal DB = ek shop ka register (exact, par ek jagah). NewSQL = mall ka central booking jo 50 counters par ACID se chalta — kisi bhi counter par ticket transaction atomic. Cockroach = register ka computer system PG jaisa par counters + replicas, Raft manager. Spanner = Google ka super system — counters jude, atomic clock global.
lessons.why: Interview: "SQL kisi scale par?" — NewSQL answer. Spanner TrueTime ka novelty + Raft internals. Ye distributed-SQL middle ground architect-level point hai.

visual.cap: NewSQL = full SQL + ACID, distributed. Raft replicates; TrueTime spans DCs.

lessons.name: In-memory databases — Redis, Memcached
lessons.desc: In-memory databases store data in RAM for microsecond latency. Redis supports rich data structures with AOF/RDB persistence. Memcached is simpler, multi-threaded, no persistence. 100-1000x faster than disk.
lessons.q: When would you choose Redis over Memcached?
lessons.qsub: What is the Redis eviction policy allkeys-lru? When would you use volatile-lru instead?
terms: Data RAM mein — bypass disk I/O. Redis, Memcached, SAP HANA.
RAM volatile — Redis RDB/AOF, cluster snapshot (S3).
Memory full — LRU policies se data nikaalo.
Append-only file — har write log, granular restore.
lessons.what:
In-memory databases data ko RAM mein rakhte hain — disk I/O zero, sub-millisecond. Redis sabse known: structures + TTL + optional persistence RDB (snapshot) / AOF (append log) — RAM ka jhoka agar crash, persistence wapas laata hai.

RAM limited + expensive → eviction policies (LRU: peeche wale nikaalo) + TTL. Disk-DB vs in-memory: disk = durable heavy; in-memory = speed + cache pattern. Hybrid: hot data in-memory layer, source of truth disk DB.
lessons.analogy: Chef ka counter: chhota sa counter par sab kuch turant milta (no moving to fridge). Par counter ka bhaanda bhar gaya — purana saaman peeche hatao (LRU). Raat ko door band ki (crash) — saaman gaya — isliye morning recipe list (RDB/AOF) se phir bharo. Root fridge (disk DB) slow par pakka — bada feast wahi se.
lessons.why: Caching archetype — har system design mein Redis ya Memcached. Persistence RDB vs AOF, TTL, eviction — production know-how + interview. "RAM ping kyun tez" — cache reads ka peak isi se handle hota.

lessons.name: Embedded databases — SQLite, DuckDB
lessons.desc: Embedded databases run inside your app process with no separate server. SQLite: single file, full SQL, every phone has it. DuckDB: columnar, great for running SQL analytics on CSV/Parquet files locally.
lessons.q: What are the limitations of SQLite? When does it reach its limits?
lessons.qsub: How does DuckDB differ from SQLite? Why is it better for analytics?
terms: App ke andar library — no server. SQLite, DuckDB.
SQLite concurrent reads + writer not blocked.
lessons.what:
Embedded databases app ke andar library ki tarah chalte hain — koi server, koi port, koi setup. SQLite: file-based, ultra portable (mobile, local apps, edge). DuckDB: analytical gold — columnar + parquet par direct SQL — data science ka ETL zero-copy.

Caveats: SQLite write concurrency limited (kaafi nodes single-writer) — WAL mode improves reads. Embedded vs client-server: multi-process scale = server; local/edge analysis = embedded.
lessons.analogy: Pocket diary vs bank branch: SQLite = pocket diary — apne pocket (app) mein, koi ID card nahi (no login), file hi diary. Bank branch (server DB) = formal counter, doosre apne paas. DuckDB = pocket calculator for bookkeeping — saare khate books par analysis, bina branch ke order. Large team work = branch; local math = diary.
lessons.why: Interview: "SQLite kahan?" — local cache/local-first apps. DuckDB — modern analytics tooling ka buzz. Embedded vs server trade — scale + concurrency versus simplicity.

lessons.name: Polyglot persistence — multiple DB types
lessons.desc: Polyglot persistence means using different databases for different workloads. Postgres for core data, Redis for cache, Elasticsearch for search, S3 for files. Each database excels at what it does best.
lessons.q: How do you decide which database to use for each part of your application?
lessons.qsub: How do you keep multiple databases in sync? What role does CDC play?
terms: Alag data needs = alag stores — one app, many DBs.
Relational for orders, KV for carts, search engine for products.
Har microservice apna DB — distributed txn pain.
Ek robust DB (PG JSONB tok) — minimal team size par.
Postgres JSON column — document behavior in SQL.
lessons.what:
Polyglot persistence = ek hi system, kai data stores, har use-case ko best tool: orders → Postgres, cart/session → Redis, search → Elasticsearch, analytics → ClickHouse. Fit-per-use ka naam — har workload apni tradeoff.

Cost: kai systems = kai ops + data sync (event-driven) + eventual consistency. Chhoti team → ek robust DB (Postgres+JSONB) to begin; polyglot jab patterns clear hon. Graph/vector/specialized needs hi system justify karein.
lessons.analogy: Ek aadmi ka ghar vs mansion kitchen: chhoti kitchen mein ek hi chulha (single DB) — simple. Bada ghar: alag tandoor (search), alag fridge tray (cache), register (orders). Har zone ka apna expert — par har nayi zone = naya staff + rule book. Basic ghar mein ek hi stove se kaam chalao, jab bade log aaye tab zones.
lessons.why: Interview: "why multiple databases?" — polyglot explanation + trap (premature polyglot). Ye system design ka honest answer: store per concern, not per microservice.

lessons.name: Database Migrations — schema versioning, zero-downtime, backward compatibility
lessons.desc: Database migrations version-control schema changes. Tools: Flyway (Java), Alembic (Python), Prisma Migrate (Node.js), golang-migrate. Zero-downtime: additive changes only (add column, not rename). Rollback strategy for each migration. Backward compatible: old code must work with new schema.
lessons.q: How do you perform a zero-downtime database migration? What is the expand-contract pattern?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between forward-only migrations and reversible migrations? How do you handle column renames safely?
terms: Versioned schema change — code repo mein SQL files.
lessons.what:
Migrations schema changes ko versioned, reproducible, reviewable banate hain — ad hoc SQL bolne se better. Har change ek numbered file: 001_create_users.sql. Tools (Flyway, Liquibase, ORM migrate) order mein apply karte + schema_migrations table mein record.

Golden rules: additive pehle (naya column/table) — backward compatible; remove old later. Expand & Contract: add column → deploy code → drop column. Rolling deploys ke saath ye kritik hai. Down migrations = rollback option.
lessons.analogy: Chhote-chhote commits vs bada phatka change: migrations = kitchen renovation ke chhote steps (nayi wiring add, phir purani hatao). Ek file ek idea — review karo, revert kar sakte. Bina migration — "raat ko live DB par ALTER" = pehle table kata, phir code toota. Expand & contract: nawi wire laga (additive) → sab use karo → purani hatao.
lessons.why: Interview: "schema change safely kaise?" — migrations + expand/contract. Ye production ops ka 101 — reviewable DDL, rollback story. Follow-up: auto-apply CI/CD pipeline.

lessons.name: Multi-tenancy patterns — shared DB, schema-per-tenant, DB-per-tenant
lessons.desc: Shared DB: all tenants in same tables with tenant_id column (cheapest, hardest to isolate). Schema-per-tenant: separate schemas in one DB (good isolation, moderate cost). DB-per-tenant: fully isolated (highest cost, easiest to customize). Row-Level Security (RLS) enforces tenant isolation at DB level.
lessons.q: What are the tradeoffs between shared DB, schema-per-tenant, and DB-per-tenant?
lessons.qsub: How does Row-Level Security enforce tenant isolation? When would you choose DB-per-tenant over shared DB?
terms: Ek software kai customers (tenants) — data alag se.
Pooled (shared DB, tenant_id), Schema-per-tenant, Separate DB.
Pooled model ka apna address — har query mein.
Alag schema per customer — clean boundary, ops moderate.
PG Row-Level Security — tenant_id automatically filter (bina WHERE bhule).
lessons.what:
Multi-tenancy = ek SaaS system, kai customers, data isolated. Levels: (1) pooled — ek DB, tenant_id column; cheap + simple, par WHERE bhoolna = data leak (RLS bachata hai). (2) schema-per-tenant — boundary clean, migrations zyada. (3) DB-per-tenant — max isolation + cost, enterprise.

Pick: chhote-medium users → pooled + RLS; big/regulated accounts → schema/DB per tenant. Tenant data leak = nightmare — isolation ka design pehle hi zaroori.
lessons.analogy: Apartment building rooms: pooled = ek huge common office, har zone mein apna desk + lock (tenant_id + RLS door guard — bina poochhe insaan sirf apna zone). Schema-per-tenant = har family ka apna floor (clean, unka saaman). DB-per-tenant = alag bungalow — poori ownership, mehengi. Guard (RLS) se pooled mein leak nahi hogi.
lessons.why: SaaS interview: "how isolate tenants?" — three models + tradeoff + PG RLS. Ye security + ops scaling ka important architect point. "WHERE tenant_id bhoolna" — RLS automatic guard.

lessons.name: Monitoring — pg_stat_statements, cache hit ratio
lessons.desc: Monitoring tracks key health signals. Most important metrics: query latency p95/p99, active connections, cache hit rate (>95% target), disk I/O, replication lag. PostgreSQL built-in views expose all of this.
lessons.q: What are the most important database metrics to monitor in production?
lessons.qsub: How do you use pg_stat_statements to find the slowest queries?
terms: DB health visibility — metrics, logs, dashboards.
CPU, connections, cache hit, slow queries, replication lag, disk.
Kitne ms se upar wale — tuning targets.
lessons.what:
DB monitoring = duniya ki nadi visible rakho. Metrics: CPU, connections (pool chahiye), cache hit ratio (>95%), slow queries (log mein), replication lag (seconds), disk I/O/space. Tools: pg_stat_activity, Prometheus + Grafana, CloudWatch.

Alerting se pehle hi jaano (page bloat, connection starvation), user pehle na poochhe. SLO: p95 latency, error rate. Monitoring se indexing/planning ke targets milte — guess nahi.

Alert = rule par SMS jab paani ka pressure gire. PgBouncer = ek door jisse 10 bande andar — ghar par 100 alag doors (connections) nahi.
lessons.why: Production ops core — "DB slow, pehla kya karte ho?" → metrics + slow query log. Interview practical: index from monitoring insight, pool connection, alert thresholds.

lessons.name: Connection pooling — PgBouncer, HikariCP
lessons.desc: Opening a new DB connection takes 5-100ms and PostgreSQL spawns a process. Connection pooling keeps a fixed number of connections open and reuses them. Optimal pool size is ~2x CPU cores.
lessons.q: Why is connection pooling necessary? What happens without it?
lessons.qsub: What is the optimal connection pool size? Why does more connections sometimes mean worse performance?
terms: DB connections ka reusable set — har request naya na bane.
TCP handshake + auth + memory — new conn expensive.
CPU ke aas-paas — (core*2)+disk; hazaaron conn = thrash.
PG connection pooler — transaction pooling mode.
Java default — sane defaults + fast borrow.
lessons.what:
Har query ke liye nayi DB connection banana = TCP + auth + worker + memory ka kharcha. Connection pool ready-made connections ka bucket — app borrow karta, use karta, wapas karta. Sustained throughput bina connection churn ke.

Pool size: zyada connections = zyada workers — CPU se aage nahi. Formula-ish: (core*2) + effective disk. 10k connections = memory burn + thundering herd. PgBouncer = external pooler (transaction vs session pooling).
lessons.analogy: Swimming pool ki lanes: har tairne wala naya pool khodta (new connection) — pagalpan. Pool = 20 ready lanes, aadmi le, taire, wapas de. Zyada lanes = paisa + bheed ki khoka; kam nahi. Booking agency (PgBouncer) app se lanes banaye rakhta — transaction ke liye turant.
lessons.why: Interview: "app slow — DB connection exhaustion" ka jawaab pool hai. Pool size + PgBouncer — production baseline. Ye app-scale basics ka part.

lessons.name: Backup & recovery — PITR via WAL, RPO/RTO
lessons.desc: PITR (Point-in-Time Recovery) restores to any specific moment using a base backup + archived WAL files. RPO = max data loss. RTO = recovery time. Test your backups by actually restoring them.
lessons.q: How does Point-in-Time Recovery work in PostgreSQL?
lessons.qsub: What is the difference between RPO and RTO? How do they influence backup strategy?
terms: Data ko alag jagah copy — restore ke liye.
Point-in-Time Recovery — kisi bhi moment tak restore.
Har WAL segment S3 par — continuous log.
Kitna data loss tolerance / kitni der mein up.
lessons.what:
Backup = disaster ke liye copy. PITR (PostgreSQL): base backup + WAL archiving — kisi bhi moment par restore (ghalti se delete hua data bachta hai). Full base + incremental WAL — balance.

RPO (data loss seconds?) vs RTO (back online minutes) define karo. Tested restores = asli backup (hamesha drill) — nahi to backup ka backup. Cloud: RDS snapshots + PITR built-in.
lessons.analogy: Zindagi ka diamond locker + CCTV: backup = locker mein diamond ka photo (full copy). PITR = CCTV ka feed jo har second record karta (WAL) — kisi bhi second ka moment restore (chori kis waqt hui — bata deta hai). Locker photo purani hui to CCTV se moment. Drill = har mahine "naya locker kholkar photo match karo" — bina drill backup = sirf kaghaz.
lessons.why: Interview backup: "data loss se kaise bacho?" — PITR + tested restore. RPO/RTO vocabulary senior-level signal. Ye ops ka non-negotiable.

lessons.name: Migration strategies — Expand-Migrate-Contract
lessons.desc: Schema migrations in production are dangerous. Safe strategy: Expand (add new column), Migrate (backfill in batches), Contract (drop old column). Tools like gh-ost and pgroll do online migrations with no locking.
lessons.q: What is the Expand-Migrate-Contract pattern? Why is it safer than direct ALTER TABLE?
lessons.qsub: How does gh-ost perform online schema changes on MySQL without locking?
terms: Additive first, deploy, remove old later — zero downtime.
Naya column bhi write — old readers still fine.
gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change — copy + swap, bina lock.
Direct ALTER on big table = table lock = downtime.
Naye column ko purana data — batched jobs.
lessons.what:
Zero-downtime schema change = Expand & Contract: 1) expand — additive column/table (backfill slow karo), 2) deploy code jo naya use kare, 3) contract — purana hatao. Direct ALTER bade table par = lock storm (writes ruk jaate hain).

Online tools (gh-ost, pt-osc) ghost table banate, data copy, binlog sync, swap — bina long lock. 1M+ row tables ke liye default answer.
lessons.analogy: Flyover bridge repair: direct road close = jam (lock). Expand & contract = pehle naya lane banao (additive), traffic naya lane par, phir purana band karo (drop). gh-ost = construction jisme chhote nudges kaap mein hote; live traffic nahi rukta. Backfill = purane data ko naye format mein bharna — batches mein, block nahi.
lessons.why: Interview: "add a column to huge table without downtime?" — expand/contract + online DDL tools. Ye production migrations ka senior answer — lock storms se bacha.

lessons.name: Security — SQL injection, RBAC, RLS
lessons.desc: SQL injection is the #1 database attack. ALWAYS use parameterized queries. RBAC gives minimum required privileges. Row-Level Security in PostgreSQL enforces which rows each user can see at the database level.
lessons.q: How do you prevent SQL injection? Why are parameterized queries essential?
lessons.qsub: How does Row-Level Security work in PostgreSQL for multi-tenant applications?
terms: App ke SQL mein attacker ka chhupa code ghusana.
Query ka skeleton + params alag — SQL parse fixed.
Values bind, kabhi string concat nahi.
Row Level Security — row visibility per policy.
Sirf utna access jitna kaam ka.
lessons.what:
SQL injection = SQL ke andar attacker ka chhupa code: WHERE email = 'admin' OR '1'='1' — kabhi string concatenation se query nahi banao. Prepared statements key: SQL skeleton pehle parse, phir values bind — injection impossible (values kabhi SQL nahi banti).

Access: RBAC — user/role permission mapping; RLS — SQL row gating (multi-tenant). Least privilege — app user ko DROP na do. Sanitization = second ring; param binding = main door.
lessons.analogy: Ticket counter par "naam batao": concat = counter wala naam seedha register likhta — naam "Rahul; sab paise de do" likha to register par rakam chalke (injection!). Prepared — pehle form (soch lo) fixed, naam sirf value box mein — "Rahul;..." value hi, command nahi. RLS = har khidki ka apna door, key (policy) sirf apna group utha sakta.
lessons.why: Security interview pehla — SQLi yaad hai? Prepared statements + ORM ka safe path. RLS/RBAC = access-level sophistication. Ye ek hi line mein "how would you secure DB" ka complete answer.

visual.cap: String concat = injection door khula. Prepared = params par, SQL fixed. RLS gates rows.

lessons.name: N+1 problem — detection, eager loading, DataLoader
lessons.desc: The N+1 problem: load a list (1 query) then load details for each item (N queries). 100 posts + comments = 101 queries. Fix: eager loading with JOINs or batch loading with DataLoader.
lessons.q: What is the N+1 query problem? How do you detect and fix it?
lessons.qsub: How does DataLoader in JavaScript batch database queries within a single event loop tick?
terms: 1 query root + N queries children — kaafi network hops.
Pehle se children le aao — ORM joins/with.
IN (ids...) — children ko ek query mein.
lessons.what:
N+1: root ke 1 record ke liye ek query, phir 100 records ke liye 100 queries — slow. Example: SELECT posts + har post ke liye SELECT comments.

Fixes: JOIN (rows flat — pagination yaad), batch WHERE id IN (...), ORM eager loading (with/eager), DataLoader-style queue batching. Keval read path — write path rare.
lessons.analogy: Kirana delivery: N+1 = har ghar ke liye alag rickshaw (N rickshaws) — wahiyaat. Batch = ek rickshaw poore gaon ki list (WHERE city IN) — ek trip. JOIN = ek hi challan jisme saaman + receipts dono. DataLoader = pehle sab orders ikattha karo phir ek baar delivery. Network hops kam = app fast.
lessons.why: Interview "app slow API kyun?" — N+1 classic. ORM eager loading + batch IN — correct answer. Ye performance debugging ka sabse common performance bug bhi hai.

lessons.name: URL Shortener DB — sharding, caching, pre-generated keys
lessons.desc: URL shortener maps short codes to long URLs. Read-heavy (99% reads). Shard by short code hash. Cache hot URLs in Redis. Pre-generate codes to avoid uniqueness checks on each write.
lessons.q: How would you design the database layer for a URL shortener at scale?
lessons.qsub: Why would you pre-generate short codes in batches instead of generating on each write?
terms: Alag URLs same short code — unique row pehle.
Sab used codes ka set — collision check fast.
lessons.what:
URL shortener design (tinyurl): POST long URL → return abc123; GET /abc123 → 301 Location redirect. Storage: short_code PK + long_url + created_at + clicks.

Code: auto-increment id → base62 encode (short, no ugly chars). DB: mapping table (hash key = code). Caching: hot URLs Redis (read-heavy: 99% reads). Expiry/cleanup + analytics counters. Collision: same long URL → upsert same code. Hash (MD5) + prefix = common — collisions handle karo.
lessons.analogy: Pustakalaya ki chhoti slip: lambe naam ki jagah emal karo "shelf-code" — chhota. "Aao 12B3" slip lekar dekhte: table se join, long naam do (redirect). Cache-se 301 = baar-baar reserve nahi. Writer (0.1%, write) se kaam koi — reader (99.9%) sab hash zone.
lessons.why: System design ka classic — scale calcs (reads/writes), storage, cache, redirect semantics. Hash vs base62, collision, TTL — har interview mein aata.

lessons.name: Chat/Messaging DB — conversation partitioning, ordering
lessons.desc: Chat needs message ordering per conversation, low latency delivery. Shard by conversation ID so all messages in one chat stay together. Use sequence numbers per conversation for ordering.
lessons.q: How do you ensure message ordering in a distributed chat system?
lessons.qsub: Why shard by conversation ID instead of user ID? What are the trade-offs?
terms: WebSocket push — bade scale par LB + fan-out.
Ek message kai receivers ko — queues/read replicas.
lessons.what:
Chat system design: send message → store (Postgres/Cassandra) + push via WebSocket. conversation_id fixed slot; messages ORDER BY ts. Fan-out: group chat = message to N members — queue at scale.

Storage choices: 1:1 chat = single row per message; group big threads = shared + cursor (no per-member copy). Unread counts = Redis counters. Presence = heartbeat → Redis TTL, online list. Read receipts = last_read_ts per user.
lessons.analogy: Hostel mess notice board + messenger: likha (store), turant announcement (WebSocket) group ke sabko. Message ek baar likha, sab apne inbox se padhe — per-person copy nahi (shared doc + cursor). Unread = "kaunsi line tak padha" per member (Redis counter). Online = "aakhri 2 min mein kya kiya" heartbeat se.
lessons.why: System design favourite — WhatsApp/Discord jaisa. Real-time, fan-out, presence, unread — multi-component design ka best practice. Derives microservices + queues + cache.

lessons.name: News Feed DB — push vs pull, celebrity handling
lessons.desc: Push (fan-out on write): copy post to all follower feeds — fast reads, expensive for celebrities. Pull (on read): fetch from followed users — expensive reads. Hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities.
lessons.q: What is the difference between fan-out-on-write and fan-out-on-read?
lessons.qsub: How do Twitter and Instagram handle celebrity accounts with millions of followers?
terms: Har user ka personalized timeline — posts from followed.
Post time hi followers ke feeds mein daal do — read cheap.
Serve samay merge — hot users ok, celebs bhi fine.
Redis list per user — precomputed timeline.
lessons.what:
News feed design = har user ka personal timeline. Fan-out on write: post aate hi followers ke Redis lists mein daal do — reads fast; par celeb? 100M followers = 100M writes. Fan-out on read: read par influencer feeds merge karo — hot users fast, celebs cheap. Hybrid best: normal = write-fanout, celebrity = read-merge.

Feed cache: per-user Redis list (post ids) + hydrate details (cache + DB). Ranking: recency × engagement. Pagination: cursor by id.
lessons.analogy: Chai tapri group ki khabar chain: fan-out-on-write = khud har dost ke ghar pehle se bhejo (milte hi turant sab khabar) — par superstar news har jagah = thakaan. Read-merge = bade logon ka sirf read par. Hybrid = regular doston ki pre-list, celebrities read-par check. Timeline = calendar; cursor = unread marks.
lessons.why: Twitter/IG design interview ka epic prashn — fan-out strategies + Redis feed + ranking. Distributed caching + event-driven ka complete jaal. "Why not just DB query?" — friends merge per request kathin.
